# CodeYourPCB tracker - the control center

Last updated: 2026-08-24. Update after every material step: add to DONE, pull the next item into NEXT-ACTION, in the same commit as the change.

Read this file first. It is the source of truth for what is in flight and what comes next.

## Where the project stands

- Version 0.2.0-beta, ~44k lines (Rust workspace + TypeScript viewer). Last release commit `746bd63` (2026-04-15).
- GSD milestones M001-M005 are marked complete in `.gsd/STATE.md`. That status was written in March and predates the 2026-07-10 audit, which ran the code and found crash-tier defects. **Where the two disagree, the audit wins** - it executed commands, the milestone summaries did not.
- Development happens in the `code-server` container on the build host (12 cores, 10GB cap). Full clean release build: 34s. Full debug build: 20s.

## Vectors (parallel branches - keep ALL moving)

### V8 - Stackup parity with KiCad and Altium

- DONE: **a copper pour named after its net was dropped on import, and the grammar was the reason.** `zone_definition` took an **identifier** for the zone name while `zone_net` had already learned about quotes, so a board with a `GND` plane and a `VBUS+` plane came back with one of them and `// one zone named "VBUS+" is not written: the grammar takes an identifier for a zone name and has no quoted form` where the other should have been. A pour is usually named after the net it fills, and the net that most often needs quoting is the power rail.
- **One rule, three places.** `net_name` - the choice of an identifier or a quoted string - is now what the zone name takes in `grammar/grammar.js` (regenerated with `npx tree-sitter generate`), in the hand-written reader, and in `dsl.rs`, which no longer has a branch for describing what it could not write. Measured on the fixture: `zone GND {` bare and `zone "VBUS+" {` quoted, each in the form its own name needs.
- **The README said a pour `has no syntax in the language yet`.** It has had one; what it lacked was a name it could keep. The feature table now says what the command does, and the fixture that proves it is the USB board from the run before this one, which now carries both planes as well as its named pads.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test a_pour_named_after_its_net_comes_back` -> **3 passed**, including the layer and net of each plane, because a pour that comes back on the wrong layer is copper in the wrong place. Both readers still agree: `cargo test -p cypcb-parser --features tree-sitter-parser --test differential` -> **3 passed**, `--test error_parity` -> **5 passed**. Mutations, each alone against a clean tree and restored from the saved file: the reader's zone name back to `identifier` -> **3 failed**, the import stops because what it wrote will not read back; the writer emitting the zone name bare -> **3 failed**, the same way. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **that action was written on a false premise, and checking it first turned up the real loss.** The importer does **not** flatten a pour: `axis_aligned_rectangle` refuses anything that is not four corners, saying `is a 6-point outline; this importer carries rectangular pours only, and a bounding box would put copper where the shape was drawn to avoid it`. What was wrong is who heard it. `cypcb-render` prints `metadata.zone_refusals` in the browser; `cypcb from-kicad` printed nothing, so a board came through the command line one ground plane short and said `Wrote ... 2 component(s), 3 net(s), 2 footprint definition(s)` as if nothing had happened.
- **The command reports both refusal lists now**, zones and stackup, on stderr beside the summary. The fixture carries an L-shaped ground plane cut around the receptacle, so the same file holds two pours that arrive and one that cannot.
- Proof: `./target/release/cypcb from-kicad tests/fixtures/usb_c_named_pads.kicad_pcb` -> `Warning: the zone on net GND is a 6-point outline; ...`, where the same command printed only the summary before. `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test a_pour_the_importer_cannot_carry_is_named` -> **2 passed**. Mutations, each alone against a clean tree and restored from the saved file: the reporting loop removed -> **1 failed**; `axis_aligned_rectangle` approximating any outline by its bounding box -> **2 failed**, both the missing warning and `the design has exactly two` pours. The first attempt at that second mutation dropped only the four-point guard and **passed**, because the corner check refuses a six-point outline on its own - the test said so by not moving. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **a board that goes to KiCad and back walked off its own outline, and the second trip is where it showed.** Pads, traces, vias and pours are all read relative to the board's corner - the model puts that corner at zero, because KiCad lays boards out anywhere on a sheet - and `extract_board_ring` read the edge in **file** coordinates. Measured on the USB fixture: `from-kicad`, `to-kicad`, `from-kicad` again moved every part 10mm left and 5mm up while the outline stayed on the sheet at 141mm, 100mm, and a third trip would move it again. `extract_board_ring` takes the same origin as everything else now, and the two designs are byte-identical.
- **The first import was right, which is why nothing caught it.** Every existing test imports once. The round trip had never been run twice, and the loss is invisible until it is - which is the same shape as the stale-binary reading in V1: the measurement, not the code, was what nobody had repeated.
- **Both ways of writing an edge are held now.** KiCad writes loose `gr_line` segments, which is also what this project's writer emits, and a `gr_poly` ring for a polygon - a form no fixture here had, so the test writes one: a 40 by 25 board with a bite out of its bottom left, whose ring has to come back at the board's corner rather than the sheet's.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test the_round_trip_puts_the_board_back_where_it_was` -> **3 passed**; `diff` of the design before and after a full trip through KiCad -> empty, where it was four outline points and every part before. `cargo test --workspace --exclude cypcb-desktop` -> no failures. Mutations, each alone against a clean tree and restored from the saved file: the origin dropped from the segment branch -> **2 failed**, `the outline came back somewhere else`; dropped from the polygon branch -> **1 failed**, `the ring is written from the board's corner, not from the sheet's`. The polygon mutation passed against the first draft of that test, whose fixture was a plain rectangle - an outline equal to the board's own box is not written at all, so there was nothing to be wrong. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **the census was taken, and the first line of every example's loss list was the board's own name.** With the trip stable, `to-kicad` plus `from-kicad` over `examples/*.cypcb` and a line diff shows what the pair costs. Every design came home as `board KiCad_PCB` - `blink`, `cutout`, `mains_sequencer`, all of them - and no warning mentioned it, because nothing knew it was a loss.
- **KiCad has no field for a board's name and does have a title block**, which is where pcbnew puts the name a person reads, so that is where this project writes it and where it reads it back. A board pcbnew wrote states nothing there and still arrives as `KiCad PCB`, which is the half that keeps this from being a rename. Measured: `to-kicad examples/blink.cypcb` -> `(title_block (title "blink"))`, and back -> `board blink {`, where the same pair produced `board KiCad_PCB {` before.

A diff that ignores formatting is the instrument the next pass needs.

Mutations, each alone against a clean tree and restored from the saved file: the title block dropped from the writer -> **1 failed**; `extract_title` ignored on the way in -> **1 failed**, `and it has to come home under its own name`. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.

- DONE: **`export` drops exactly one thing a design can state, and it said nothing about it.** The Gerber job file's material stackup is specified as the layers of the bare board and only those, so `material_type` returns nothing for a **stiffener** - bonded on after the stack is pressed, like solder paste is deposited at assembly. Right about the file, wrong in silence: a design that states one is asking for a board nobody can make from that set of files alone. What is left in this direction needs evidence this repo does not have: how KiCad assigns a net to a class, which would let width and clearance travel in the project file.

The owner asked for all seven gaps found on 2026-08-23 while reading this
project's stackup against what KiCad and Altium can state. Ordered as they were
answered, not as they were found. Every one of them is closed.

1. **What the fabricator does to the board** - **DONE**, see below.
   - **Units** - **DONE**, see below. (Listed as item 4 when the list was
     written; taken second because every other item on it states a number.)
2. ~~**Colour of mask and silkscreen.**~~ **DONE.**
3. ~~**Dielectric sub-layers.**~~ **DONE.**
4. ~~**Units.**~~ **DONE.**
5. ~~**An impedance solver.**~~ **DONE.** Every item on this list is closed.
6. ~~**Drill pairs and sequential lamination.**~~ **DONE.**
7. ~~**Rigid-flex.**~~ **DONE.**

- DONE (item 1): **the five things KiCad states about a board that this project
  read and walked past.** `copper_finish`, `edge_plating`, `castellated_pads`,
  `edge_connector` and `dielectric_constraints` live inside KiCad's own
  `(stackup ...)`, and `pcb_parser.rs` said in a comment that it passed over
  them. A board imported from KiCad and sent back out asked for a different
  build than it arrived with, and nothing said so.
- **The language says them now**, in the block where they are bought:
  `finish "ENIG"`, `edges plated`, `pads castellated`, `connector bevelled`,
  `impedance controlled`. Each is a statement and silence is the rest, the way
  `locked` on a trace is. Both readers, `sync`, the DSL writer, the KiCad
  importer and the KiCad writer all carry them.
- **The contradiction this closes was in the checker, not in the format.**
  `DesignConstraints::castellated_holes_allowed` has been in every fab table
  since the tables were written, and `DesignRules::from_constraints` dropped it
  before it reached any rule - so a flag every house sets checked nothing, and
  no board could state the want either. Both halves exist now, and
  `StackupRule` reports a board asking for castellated pads against a table
  that does not make them.
- **`(edge_plating no)` is read as no.** pcbnew leaves a flag out when it is
  off, so the node being present is nearly the statement - but the explicit
  `no` does occur, and reading presence as `yes` would order plating nobody
  asked for.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-world --test what_the_board_block_survives` ->
  **13 passed**; `cargo test -p cypcb-kicad --test the_kicad_board_carries_the_stackup`
  -> **15 passed**; `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test the_stackup_has_to_match_the_board`
  -> **13 passed**. Read off the release binary: a board with all five states
  `the stackup asks for castellated pads and this table does not make them`.
  Mutations, each alone against a clean tree: `sync` dropping the flag -> 1
  failed; the DSL writer dropping its line -> 1 failed; the KiCad writer
  dropping `(edge_plating yes)` -> 1 failed; the importer reading `no` as
  `yes` -> 1 failed; the rule's condition inverted -> 2 failed;
  `from_constraints` hard-coding the flag to `false` -> 1 failed.
  `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- **The gate itself needed a fix to get there.** `playwright.config.ts` served
  the viewer on 4321, which is Astro's default, and another repository's dev
  server in this container held it - so stage 6 failed on a port rather than on
  the code. `CYPCB_E2E_PORT` overrides it and the default is 4327, with
  `--strictPort` so a busy port fails loudly rather than moving the server
  somewhere the tests are not looking.
- DONE (item 4): **copper is stated in the unit it is bought in.** `um` is a
  length like the rest. `oz` is not: it is a weight per square foot, so it is
  taken in one position - a stackup's copper layer - and refused everywhere
  else. `size 1oz x 2oz` is not a board and `core 1oz` is not a dielectric;
  the second says what ounces are rather than leaving the loop to answer
  "`stackup` has no property `oz`".
- **One conversion, in one place.** `cypcb_core::NM_PER_OZ` is 34,998 - one
  ounce over a square foot is 1.378 mils - and `cypcb-calc`'s IPC-2221 width
  calculation now derives its `MILS_PER_OZ` from it instead of carrying its
  own copy. Two copies is how the thickness a trace is priced on drifts from
  the thickness the board is built with.
- **A thickness comes back in the unit it was written in.** `StackupLayer`
  gained `written_as`, which is presentation and not a second truth: the
  number is always nanometres. A stackup that says `copper 1oz` reads
  `copper 1oz` after a save rather than `copper 0.034998mm`, because a
  fabricator asked for an order rather than for arithmetic. Millimetres still
  print at six decimals, which is 1nm resolution and what makes the round trip
  exact.

  ordinary case. `sheet 0.0668mm material "FR4" dk 4.5` on the same entry;
  KiCad calls it `addsublayer` and this project read the layer and dropped the
  rest, so a six-layer board came back thinner than it went out.
- **Two things that read a dielectric now read the slot.** `slot_thickness`
  sums every sheet and `Stackup::total_thickness` uses it - that figure is the
  depth every plated hole is drilled through and what a fab quotes against.
  `slot_dk_x1000` answers `None` when the sheets disagree, so a slot pressed
  from two laminates reports as **not checked** rather than checked against
  whichever sheet came first. The layer's own `thickness` still means its own
  first sheet, so nothing that read it has silently changed meaning.

  blind or buried from the board's own copper count and reports the last two
  where the table refuses them.

  in the stackup is a drill pair - what Altium's stack manager calls one, and
  what KiCad has no word for. A via whose span is not on the list is a hole
  this build does not make, whatever the house is capable of; a board that
  lists none is asked only the fab table's question.

  `zone` or a `keepout`, and it is neither: copper crosses a flexible region,
  that is what it is for.
- **One rule, and it is the one every flex design guide leads with.**
  `FlexHoleRule` (`flex-hole`, rule registry 28) reports a drilled hole inside
  a flexible region: the barrel of a plated hole is a tube of copper on the
  wall, the laminate around it moves every time the board is folded and the
  barrel does not, so it work-hardens and splits. A board that declares no
  region is never asked, which is every board this project shipped.

  pour of another net. Both read `is_copper_pour()` now.

- **D8, V1: the clearance rule keeps counting pairs of segments. The contact
  count is published beside it.** Three reasons, in the order they weigh. A
  violation is a *place*: two segments of one trace touching a pad at two
  points are two places a fabricator's etch can fail, and collapsing them in
  the model throws the locations away. The counts are *regression ratchets*
  before they are a report, and a per-contact count is the coarser number - it
  would mask a routing change that a per-segment count catches, which is the
  opposite of what a ratchet is for. And the reader's actual complaint - one
  problem printed 24 times - was answered four runs ago on all three surfaces
  without moving a single number. What was missing was never a different count
  but a second one.
- **D9, V7: the bucket queue is refused.** A 9.45% profile saving is
  approximately 0.4 seconds on a benchmark that takes seconds; `qfp_fanout`
  reading 58 shorts worse is a router that is worse at routing. Speed is a
  convenience and routing quality is the product. The tie order is also not
  incidental - `router-is-repeatable` is a gate stage, and the total order the
  heap gives is what makes it hold. The safe half of that work already shipped:
  the packed `u64` key, 2.89%, every board byte-identical. What is left needs
  an approach that keeps the total order, and until somebody has one this is
  not a trade worth making.

### V1 - CLI and core correctness
- DONE: **the two DRC paths never disagreed. The binary I measured them with was three commits old.** `cypcb check` was recorded here as reporting `clearance: 4` where the library reported 6 on the same board. Built from the same commit, both report **10 violations with 6 clearance rows**: `git checkout -- crates/cypcb-cli/src/commands/check.rs && cargo build --release && ./target/release/cypcb check /tmp/au_board.cypcb` -> `10 DRC violation(s) against jlcpcb_standard_2layer` / `clearance: 6`. The 4 was the reading of a `target/release/cypcb` last linked before `d47affd`, the commit that gave a `from ... via ... to` trace its copper back - the copper those two extra clearance rows are between. The command was right; the measurement compared a new library against an old binary.
- **The fix that entry proposed was a no-op and is not in the tree.** The diagnosis had reached "`check`'s `.cypcb` path never rebuilds the spatial index from the footprint library, unlike `export`, `route`, `score` and the KiCad path", and a rebuild was added in `run()`. `sync_ast_to_world` already does it on its way out - `crates/cypcb-world/src/sync.rs:768`, `// Rebuild spatial index after all entities are added` - so the line changed nothing, which is exactly what the mutation said: removed again, the board still read 10 and 6. Reverted. A grep for callers of `rebuild_spatial_index_from_library` reads as a hole in `check.rs` and is not one.
- **What the run leaves behind is the guard the count never had.** `check.rs` says in as many words that its header and per-kind tally stay row counts while clearance rows are grouped by contact for display, because every published figure in this project - the ratchets, the noise bands, `docs/routing.md`, every sweep table - is a count of rows. Nothing held it to that. `crates/cypcb-cli/tests/check_counts_what_the_rules_count.rs` asks the binary and asks the rules on one board that violates both counts, and requires the same answer.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test check_counts_what_the_rules_count` -> **1 passed**. Mutations, each alone against a clean tree and restored from the saved file: the per-kind tally counted after the grouping `continue` instead of before it -> **1 failed**, `the rules find 6 clearance rows and the command has to report 6`; the header printing `drc.violations.len() - 1` -> **1 failed**, `the rules find 10 and the command has to report 10`. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **`score` and `check` count the same board the same way, and the two published names mean two different things.** The commands build their rules differently - `check` runs `preset.rules()`, `score` runs `DesignRules::from_constraints(&preset.constraints())`, and that constructor has dropped fields before - so their agreeing was a fact nobody had measured since the two differed by a factor of six. On a board that breaks 10 rules in 6 clearance rows describing 3 contacts, `check` prints `10 DRC violation(s)` and `clearance: 6`, and `score` prints `"drc_violations": 10` and `"clearance_contacts": 3`.
- **The fixture is chosen so the three numbers are all different.** Rows 10, clearance rows 6, contacts 3, asserted in that order before anything else runs: a board where rows and contacts happen to be equal would let either name drift into the other and no test would notice. `clearance_contacts` had a unit test in `cypcb-drc` (`what_a_published_count_counts`); what it did not have was a check that the command shipping it under that name ships the contact count and not the row count.

- DONE: **`within` answers now, and the example about assertions stopped failing on its own assertions.** Found by running the release binary over every shipped example rather than by reading anything: twenty-three files, and the only unexpected line was `v2-constraints.cypcb` reporting **3 assertion violations** - on the example whose whole subject is assertions.
- **The old answer was reading a harder question than the one asked.** Every `within` replied `assertion not checked: within needs tolerances, which the board model does not carry yet`. A part's own manufacturing tolerance really is not in the model, and it is not what the assertion asks for: `R1.value within 10kohm +/- 5%` asks whether the value the design **states** falls in a band, and the value and the band are both in the file. Two of the example's three now hold.
- **Three bands, and the range one is not a spread.** `+/- 5%` and `+/- 0.1kohm` are spreads either side of the nominal; `within 100nF to 220nF` runs **from** the nominal **to** the stated end, so 90nF is outside it. The edges are inside the band, which is what a tolerance means.
- **What is still refused is refused for itself.** The example's third assertion, `U1.output within 3.3V +/- 0.1V`, now says `'U1.output' is not something the checker can read yet` and lists what it does know - `board.width`, `board.height`, `board.layers`, `<part>.value`, `<net>.current/width/clearance`. A band with no tolerance says what a band looks like. A resistance compared against a capacitance is refused rather than compared.
- **The rest of the example sweep was clean**, which is worth recording because it is the first time it has been run: every other file's violations are `unconnected-pin` and `unrouted-pin` - correct for boards nobody routed - except `drc-test.cypcb`, which is deliberately faulty and whose name says so. `four-layer.cypcb` reports `against jlcpcb_standard_4layer`, which is the layer-count fix from earlier today working on a real example.

- DONE: **the impedance rule was measuring the first inner layer against the top layer's surroundings, and the "no copper reaches" report from last run was my own board being wrong.** Both halves of last run's next action, diagnosed before anything was changed.
- **`Layer::Inner` is zero-based and the stack's copper sequence is not.** `sync.rs` maps the language's `Inner1` to `Layer::Inner(0)`, `job.rs` names that one `In1` and the KiCad writer spells it `In1.Cu`. The stack's sequence starts at the **top** layer, so the first inner layer is copper entry 1. `copper_index` read `Inner(n)` as entry `n`, so a trace on `Inner1` was given the top layer's dielectric and the top layer's foil. On the centred fixture the right answer is a stripline at **40.69 ohm** and the wrong one a microstrip at **64.37 ohm**.
- **It passed its own tests, and the reason is the one that has now hidden three index errors here.** A symmetric stack gives neighbouring layers the same answer, so the existing inner-layer test - written with `Inner(1)`, which is the *second* inner layer - could not tell entry 2 from entry 1. The same shape hid `BottomCopper` reading as the top last run, and the outer-layer direction the run before. The new test asserts a number a neighbouring layer cannot produce.
- **The other half was not a defect.** Last run's board reported `R1.2 is on a net that no copper reaches` for a trace on `Inner1`, and the note recorded it as observed rather than diagnosed. It is correct behaviour: the parts were 0402, so their pads are on the top layer only, and inner copper genuinely cannot reach them without a via. `sync.rs` carries a comment about exactly this - through-hole pads exist on every layer and used to not, which is what made `examples/four-layer.cypcb` report all four pins unreached. Nothing to fix.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test what_the_stack_delivers_against_what_the_net_asked_for` -> **8 passed**, the new one pinning 40.69 ohm and refusing 64.37. Mutations, each alone and reverted: the offset removed -> 1 failed; the offset doubled -> 1 failed. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- NEXT-ACTION: **a symmetric fixture cannot catch an index error, and this project has now learned that three times.** Every one of those was found by a mutation or by running the binary, never by the test that was supposed to cover it. The cheap structural answer is a fixture whose layers are all different from each other - a lopsided stack in the shared test data rather than one written per test file - so that any rule reading a layer index is asserting against a number only the right layer produces. Two test files already build their own; a third will be written the same way unless the fixture is somewhere they both reach.

The 0.250mm above is this tool's own value, not the fab's.` Under `prototype`, which states 0.5mm of its own, the same violation gets no note.

Three tests in `crates/cypcb-cli/tests/a_number_the_fab_never_stated_says_so.rs` hold all three halves: the derived rule says so, the stated one is left alone, and a rule that did not fire is not mentioned. Mutation-checked: with the provenance test dropped so every fired rule gets a note, `a_rule_the_preset_states_is_left_alone` fails.
- Observed once and not reproduced: one gate run reported `101 passed` and a failed Playwright stage without naming the spec; the standalone suite and two later gate runs are green at 102. Recorded rather than explained - if it comes back, the name is what to capture.
- DONE: **a four-layer board went to the fabricator claiming L1 twice.** Gerber X2 puts the layer in the file - `TF.FileFunction,Copper,L2,Inr` - and it is how a CAM system knows which foil goes where. Measured by exporting a four-layer board and reading the attribute out of each copper file: `F_Cu` said `Copper,L1,Top`, **`In1_Cu` said `Copper,L1,Inr`**, `In2_Cu` said `Copper,L2,Inr`, `B_Cu` said `Copper,L4,Bot`. Two files claimed L1 and **nothing claimed L3**. The same four files now read L1, L2, L3, L4.
- **Two conventions meeting, and neither was wrong on its own.** `Layer::Inner` is zero-based everywhere in this workspace - the DSL writes `inner1`, `sync.rs` reads it as `Inner(0)`, `to_copper_mask` shifts by `2 + n` - and the export computed the Gerber number as `n + 1`, which is the formula for a one-based index, with a comment saying "L2 for first inner". The comment described what it was supposed to do. `CopperSide::Inner` says which convention it takes now, and its fallback was wrong in the same way.
- **And the same directory of files described two projects.** `copper.rs` and `mask.rs` read the board's size and threw it away for the literal string `"board"` - `world.board_info().map(|(_size, _)| "board")` - while `silk.rs` and `outline.rs` used `world.board_name()`. Measured on one export: `G04 Board: board` in the copper and mask files, `G04 Board: stacked` in the silkscreen and outline. All six read `stacked` now.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test every_copper_file_says_which_layer_it_is` -> 4 passed, and with `n + 1` put back three of the four fail with `left: [1, 1, 2, 4]` against `right: [1, 2, 3, 4]` and `got ["board", "board", "board", "flight_controller", ...]`. The whole crate was green before this test existed: **131 unit tests and six integration suites, and not one of them read a file function out of an exported file.**
- **The first version of the duplicate check passed on the defect.** It deduplicated whole attribute strings, and `Copper,L1,Top` and `Copper,L1,Inr` are different strings for the same layer - which is the fault itself. It compares layer numbers now, and fails on the mutant with `two files claim the same layer - [1, 2, 4]`.
- DONE: **the export writes a Gerber job file, and the stackup finally reaches the person who presses the board.** A directory of Gerbers says what to image on each layer and nothing about the board - how thick it is, what goes between the copper, which file is which. `<board>-job.gbrjob` is Ucamco's answer and this project wrote none: 15 files before, 16 now. Measured on a board declaring a seven-layer stackup: `BoardThickness 1.57`, `LayerNumber 4`, eleven `FilesAttributes` entries, and a `MaterialStackup` that names every layer the design stated.
- **The format was read before it was written.** `gerber-job-format-specification-revision-2020-08` off Ucamco, converted with `pdftotext` and grepped, rather than copied from memory - which caught two things a plausible implementation gets wrong. A file function spells it `Soldermask` and a material stackup entry spells it `SolderMask`; the first version matched the stackup spelling against a file function and called **every mask Positive**, which is a board that comes back with solder mask over its pads. The specification's own example says `"FileFunction": "Soldermask,Top"` with `"FilePolarity": "Negative"`, and this exporter images the openings, so Negative is right.
- **The other thing the spec is strict about**: *"If the Material Stackup is included, it must be complete - all layers of the PCB, must be present."* A design states its dielectrics and says nothing about mask or silkscreen, so writing the declaration straight through would claim a board with no solder mask in the same file that lists two solder mask Gerbers. The surfaces the export actually wrote are added around the declaration, with no thickness and no colour because neither is known - and a design that does describe its own mask or silk is passed through untouched.
- **What is deliberately absent, because there is no data for it**: `Finish`, `DesignRules`, and `Material` on any dielectric. FR4 is the usual answer and nobody has told this tool. `BoardThickness` appears only when every declared layer states a thickness - a sum missing a term is not a measurement - and `MaterialStackup` only when the design declares one.
- **Nothing in the file is recomputed from what the exporter meant to write.** Each entry's `FileFunction` is read back out of the Gerber it describes, so the job file cannot disagree with the files it ships beside. The same property would have shown last fire's four-layer numbering fault in a second place.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test the_job_file_describes_the_board_it_ships_with` -> 8 passed, including the two controls (no stackup declared, partial thicknesses) and `every_gerber_written_is_named_in_the_job_file`, which compares the array against `read_dir` of the output; `cargo test -p cypcb-export --lib jobfile` -> 4 passed; `cargo run -p cypcb-cli -- export` -> `Export complete: 16 files`, `stk-job.gbrjob (2.8 KB)`, mask polarity `Negative` both sides.
- **One existing test had to be corrected rather than worked around.** `every_example_reaches_the_files` requires every file in the output whose extension starts with `g` to carry `M02*` and `%FSLAX` - and `gbrjob` starts with a g. The job file is JSON describing the Gerbers rather than a Gerber, so the filter was wrong, not the new file: 2 failed with `no end-of-file marker` across every example, 2 passed after excluding the extension by name.
- DONE: **the drill files say what they drill, and the job file names them.** Measured first, as the note below asked: the Excellon files carried no attributes at all - `M48`, a generator comment, coordinates. Every other file this exporter writes has stated a `TF.FileFunction` for as long as it has existed. So the job file described eleven Gerbers and no drill file, which reads as a board with no holes. The drill header now carries `TF.GenerationSoftware`, `TF.CreationDate` and `TF.FileFunction` as `; #@!` comments, which is where NC formats carry Gerber attributes, and the job file reads them back the same way it reads a Gerber - one mechanism, no second source of truth.
- **The span is the half that decides where the holes go.** A through file on a four-layer board states `Plated,1,4,PTH`; the non-plated file states `NonPlated,1,4,NPTH`; a via between the inner pair states `Plated,2,3,Buried` and one from the top to the first inner layer states `Plated,1,2,Blind`. A drill file with no stated span means "through everything" to every fabricator, which is what a buried via file used to look like.
- **The layer numbering now exists once.** `gerber::header::copper_layer_number` is the single place that turns a `Layer` into a Gerber layer number, called by the copper files and by the drill span. Two copies of that arithmetic is exactly how the first inner layer came to claim L1 alongside the top copper last fire.
- **Writing the drill entry exposed a flaw in what shipped last fire.** The job file sat in `gerber/` and named files by bare filename, which cannot resolve `drill/board-PTH.drl` from there. It sits at the root of the output now and names files relative to itself - `gerber/board-F_Cu.gbr`, `drill/board-PTH.drl` - and a test walks every path it claims and requires the file to be there. Every entry also carries `FileFormat` (`Gerber` or `NC`, the specification's word for Excellon), which the first version omitted entirely; a drill file described as a Gerber is one a CAM system tries to read as an image.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test the_drill_files_say_what_they_drill` -> 6 passed; `--test the_job_file_describes_the_board_it_ships_with` -> 11 passed, including `every_path_it_names_resolves_from_where_the_job_file_sits`; `cargo run -p cypcb-cli -- export` -> 16 files, `drill/stk-PTH.drl` described as `Plated,1,4,PTH` in format `NC`, eleven Gerbers with polarity and the drill file without - a file that images nothing has none, and the specification's own drill entry omits it too.
- DONE: **a design can put a part on the back of the board, which it could not do at all.** `sync.rs` carried the note - "the DSL has no word for this yet" - and derived the side from the footprint's copper, so a part was on the bottom only if its footprint had no top-side pads. No footprint in the library is built that way, so **no design could place a part on the bottom**: half of every two-sided assembly was unsayable. `side bottom` says it.
- **The flip is registered once, in the footprint library.** `mirrored_to_bottom` reverses the local x axis - a part turned over, seen from above, which is how every coordinate here is written - and moves every layer it touches to the matching layer on the other face: copper, mask, paste and silk together. `sync_ast_to_world` registers the flipped copy as `<name>@bottom` and points the instance at it, so the checker, the four Gerber writers, the drill file, the renderer and the pick-and-place list all place the mirrored pads without one of them knowing about sides. A mirror written six times is a board whose copper and solder mask disagree about which face a part is on.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test a_part_can_be_put_on_the_other_side` -> 6 passed. A bottom 0402 puts **0 flashes on F_Cu and 2 on B_Cu**, and its mask and paste move with it (0 on F_Mask/F_Paste, 2 on B_Mask/B_Paste); the CPL row says `Bottom`. Two controls: a part that states nothing and a part that states `top` produce byte-identical copper.
- **Mutation-checked, and the failure is the interesting part.** With the instance pointed back at the unflipped footprint, three tests fail with `left: 2, right: 0` on the top copper - but `the_assembly_list_tells_the_machine_which_side_to_place_it_on` still passes, because the CPL reads the `Side` component rather than the copper. That is precisely the shipping hazard this design avoids: a placement machine told `Bottom` while every pad is imaged on the top.
- **The tree-sitter grammar is updated and its generated parser is not.** `grammar.js` gains `side_property` and `parser.rs` gains the arm that reads it, so the second parser is ready; `grammar/src/parser.c` is generated from the grammar and this container has no tree-sitter CLI - `command -v tree-sitter` -> nothing, `npx tree-sitter --version` fails. The optional `tree-sitter-parser` feature is off by default (`default = ["rust-parser"]`), so this changes no build; it does mean **that parser will reject `side` until somebody regenerates it**, and the differential test - which only runs with both features on - would say so. The gate did catch the half of this that matters: `cargo test` compiles the crate with all features, so a `ComponentDef` missing the field failed the build rather than drifting quietly.
- **That NEXT-ACTION was written from a stale fact and the measurement corrected it.** It said the browser builds its own snapshot with `parseSource` in JavaScript, which stopped being true on 2026-08-07 when that reader was deleted and `WasmPcbEngineAdapter.load_source` started calling the engine. So most of the viewer needed nothing: `crates/cypcb-render/tests/a_bottom_part_reaches_the_browser_flipped.rs` drives the engine the way the browser does and a bottom part arrives with **bottom-copper layer bits and pad 1 at +0.5mm instead of -0.5mm**, and `getPadColor` already refuses to draw a bottom pad when the bottom copper is hidden.
- DONE: **the half that really was wrong is the ink.** Silkscreen and the body outline come from a footprint, and a footprint has no side of its own - the part does. The renderer drew both in the top silkscreen colour whatever side the part was on, so a bottom part printed its legend on the top of the board and looked identical to a top-side part whose pads had gone to the wrong layer. `ComponentInfo.side` now rides in the snapshot and `componentSilkColor` decides the colour; a bottom part's legend is drawn in `bottom_silk`.
- **One of the four new browser tests guards the other three.** They compare against `LAYER_COLORS.bottom_silk`, so a palette that gave both sides the same ink would leave all three passing while the screen told nobody anything; the fourth asserts the two colours differ.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-render --features native --test a_bottom_part_reaches_the_browser_flipped` -> 3 passed; `npx vitest run src/__tests__/a-bottom-part-is-drawn-as-one.test.ts` -> 4 passed.
- **The first version of the flip test was wrong about the units and said so loudly.** It subtracted the part's position from a pad coordinate that is already relative to the part, and compared -9.5mm against 10.5mm. The engine was right; the reader was not. Corrected to compare the pad against the part's own centre, with the mistake written down beside it.
- **One question a bottom part raises that this project cannot answer for itself, and will not guess.** The placement file writes the design's rotation unchanged for both faces. Our own geometry is the footprint mirrored in x and then rotated, seen from the top; viewed from the bottom - which is how a machine sees a board it is placing on the underside - that is the unmirrored footprint rotated by **minus** the same angle. So whether a fabricator's CPL wants the angle or its negative for a bottom part is a convention of theirs, not arithmetic of ours, and getting it wrong rotates every bottom part on the board. Recorded for the owner rather than picked: no board here has a rotated bottom part, so nothing is currently wrong.
- DONE: **the KiCad export described a bottom part as a front-side part with its pads on the back.** Measured by writing a board with one part on each face: `(footprint "cypcb:0402@bottom" (layer "F.Cu"))` with its reference on `F.SilkS`, its value on `F.Fab` and its pads on `B.Cu`. Three separate faults in one line - the face, the legend, and the geometry, which came from the mirrored copy this project keeps internally, so KiCad would have flipped it a second time on load. The derived name `0402@bottom` leaked into the file as well, naming a library entry nobody has.
- **The convention was not guessed.** This project's own KiCad reader relies on it and its fixture states it: a back-side footprint in a real board file carries `(layer "B.Cu")` and pad coordinates **identical** to a front-side one, because KiCad mirrors the geometry itself from the layer. So a bottom part is written from the footprint the design named, with `B.Cu`/`B.SilkS`/`B.Fab`, and `footprint::base_name` keeps the internal suffix out of the file.

With the layer choice reverted three of the five fail, and the round trip returns `[("R1", Top), ("R2", Top)]` - the part changed faces on the way through a file.

The board opened in KiCad without its ground - the same silence the Gerber writer had before the pour was implemented, one file over. It writes them now: 1 zone for that example, on `F.Cu`, net `GND`, over the rectangle the design states.

The shape came from this project's own KiCad reader and its fixture, the same authority the footprint side used.

With the writer unwired four of the five fail with `one pour went in: []`. The fifth is the control: a board with no zones still writes none.
- DONE: **the two writers disagreed about the silkscreen, and the measurement is the whole finding.** The same design through both: **38 stroked segments** in `pour-island-F_SilkS.gbr` against **0** `fp_line` in the `.kicad_pcb`. Three parts, each an outline in the fabrication files and nothing at all on screen in KiCad - so a board round-tripped through KiCad lost the marks that tell a person where its parts are. The KiCad file carries 12 now, four per part.
- **The rule is shared rather than reinvented.** `gerber/silk.rs` prints a footprint's own artwork when it has any and its courtyard outline when it does not, and `write_legend` follows the same line: artwork if present, otherwise the courtyard as four `fp_line` segments. Drawing both would put a box on the board the footprint never asked for, which is what that comment in the Gerber writer says.
- **Not checked by a round trip, and that is stated rather than papered over.** This project's KiCad reader does not read `fp_line` at all, so there is nothing to read it back with - unlike the pours and the part sides, where the reader made the round trip the strongest available proof. What is checked is the text: four lines per part, on `F.SilkS`, meeting end to end and closing; a footprint with artwork writing its artwork and no courtyard; and a board with no parts writing nothing.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-kicad --test the_board_arrives_with_its_legend` -> 4 passed; with the call unwired three fail with `left: 0, right: 4`.
- **The silkscreen import was measured and dropped rather than built.** The next step recorded last fire was to read `fp_line` back, so the legend could be round-tripped like the pours and the part sides. Counted first: the boards this project actually imports - the six routing benchmarks under `viewer/kicad-tools/boards/` - carry **0** `fp_line` and **0** `fp_circle` between them, because a script generated them. One unrelated third-party file has 25 and 3. So the reader would be tested only against a fixture written to satisfy it, which proves that it can read what I wrote and nothing else. Recorded as measured and not built.
- DONE: **two files out of the same export disagreed about how thick the board is.** `(general (thickness 1.6))` was a literal. A design declaring a stackup that sums to 1.57mm got `1.570mm of material` from the checker, `"BoardThickness": 1.57` in the Gerber job file, and **1.6** in the KiCad board - which is worse than either number being wrong on its own, because whoever notices has to work out which to believe. The KiCad file reads `Stackup::total_thickness` now, the same function the other two use.
- **1.6 stays where it is a default rather than a measurement**: a design that states no stackup, or one whose layers do not all state a thickness, keeps it, because a partial sum is not a thickness. Every example in this repository is in that case and none of them moved.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-kicad --test the_board_is_as_thick_as_the_design_says` -> 4 passed; with the literal restored two fail with `left: "1.6", right: "1.57"`. Two of the four are the controls.
- DONE: **the exported board carried no design rules at all, so KiCad checked it against KiCad's defaults.** Measured: **0** `(setup ...)` blocks in the written file. A designer opening the board and running KiCad's DRC got a different answer than `cypcb check` on the source, with neither tool saying why - the most visible form of the disagreement this export keeps producing. The file now states `min_clearance`, `min_track_width`, `min_via_diameter` and `min_through_hole`, and for `--preset jlcpcb` they read 0.127, 0.127, 0.554 and 0.3, which are the same numbers that preset gives the checker.
- **`to-kicad` was the last command in the CLI that never asked which fabricator a board is for.** `check`, `route`, `score` and `export` all take `--preset`; this one wrote a board for nobody in particular. It takes one now, and this file's older claim that "no command in the CLI guesses a fabricator" is true for the first time in the stronger sense: none of them writes fab-dependent output without being told the fab.
- **Without a preset it still writes no rules, deliberately.** Rules nobody chose are worse than none, because KiCad believes them. `cypcb-kicad` takes the four numbers as a `KicadDesignRules` argument rather than reaching for a preset table: which fab a board is for is the caller's knowledge, and the crate has no opinion about design rules.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test the_kicad_board_carries_the_rules_it_was_checked_with` -> 4 passed - the fab's own numbers, a different fab giving different numbers, no preset giving no `(setup`, and a typo refused by name. With the rules unwired two of the four fail with `no min_clearance in:`.
- DONE: **the solder mask opening was a constant in the file that goes to the fab.** Both mask sites in `job.rs` called `MaskPasteConfig::default()`, whose expansion is a hardcoded 0.05mm, so a house publishing anything else got its openings drawn to the constant - JLCPCB's four-layer rules state 0.04mm and IPC Class 2 states 0.075mm. Silently, because a mask opening a hundredth of a millimetre off looks like every other mask opening. `ExportPreset` carries `mask_expansion` now, the same discipline `silk_clearance` already had.
- **No board in this repository changes today**, and that is the honest headline: both export presets are for houses publishing 0.05mm, which is what the constant happened to be. Same shape as the copper weight - the value was right and the reason it was right was luck. A test in `cypcb-cli` now holds the export preset's number against that house's design rules, two tables in two crates that had no way to disagree loudly.
- **And the fault I wrote last fire is fixed in the same commit.** `(pad_to_mask_clearance 0)` was a literal, written one line under a comment about numbers KiCad believes. It is the fab's expansion now: `--preset jlcpcb` gives `(pad_to_mask_clearance 0.05)`.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test the_mask_opening_is_the_fabs_own` -> 3 passed, including the geometry both ways - a 0402 pad at 0.05mm gives a 0.7mm opening, at 0.04mm a 0.68mm one and no 0.7mm one; `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test the_kicad_board_carries_the_rules_it_was_checked_with` -> 5 passed.
- DONE: **every fab published a paste clearance and nothing read it.** `min_paste_clearance` appeared **thirteen times inside `cypcb-rules` and nowhere else in the workspace** - no checker, no exporter. So a board could put two SMD pads close enough that the steel between their stencil apertures tears, the openings merge and the parts bridge with solder on reflow, and every check passed. `PasteClearanceRule` is the twin of the solder mask bridge rule: same geometry, a different sheet.
- **A paste aperture is the pad itself**, because `paste_reduction` is 0.0 and a reduction is a stencil design decision rather than a number a fabricator publishes. The rule invents nothing: it reads the fab's own figure, 0.127mm for JLCPCB. A through-hole pad has no aperture at all and is skipped.
- **Measured against every bundled board before believing it**: it fires on `drc-test.cypcb` - **3 violations**, on the same overlapping pair the mask bridge rule reports - and on none of the other examples. A rule that fires on every chip resistor is a rule people turn off; an 0402's own pads sit 0.4mm apart, three times the published minimum.
- **The count was wrong the first time I read it.** `grep -c paste-clearance` said 4 because it counted the summary line `paste-clearance: 3` as well as the three violations. Corrected by listing them.
- **The new rule broke a claim the CLI makes about the board, which is the useful part.** `cypcb check` prints `copper touching copper at 0.00mm: N`, counted by filtering on `actual == 0` **regardless of kind** - so the first rule to report a different zero-width thing was counted as a short. A paste stencil web of 0.000mm is a torn stencil, not copper touching copper. The filter selects `ViolationKind::Clearance` now, and `cli_integration` went from 20 passed, 1 failed back to 21 passed.

Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test the_stencil_has_to_survive_being_made` -> 5 passed, including the two controls (a web the fab allows, and a plain 0402 board) and the through-hole case. The viewer guard caught the new kind before the table was touched: `these arrive in the panel as a raw slug: paste-clearance`.
- **Scanned every published constraint for a reader, and fifteen have none.** `blind_vias_allowed`, `board_thickness`, `buried_vias_allowed`, `castellated_holes_allowed`, `diff_pair_gap`, `diff_pair_tolerance`, `max_copper_layers`, `max_drill_aspect_ratio`, `max_stub_length`, `max_vias_per_high_speed_net`, `min_acid_trap`, `min_copper_pour_clearance`, `min_hole_to_edge`, `min_pad_size` and `min_slot_clearance` appear only inside `cypcb-rules`. Command: `grep -rn "\bFIELD\b" --include=*.rs crates/ | grep -v "^crates/cypcb-rules/"` per field.

- Before and after on `examples/pour-island.cypcb` through the real command: same 7 regions and same 29 draws, with a region edge moving `Y19600000` -> `Y19646000`. Exactly the 0.046mm, and in the direction that gives the designer the plane they asked for.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test the_pour_keeps_the_fabs_distance` -> 3 passed - every coordinate that moves, moves by 46000nm; the plane still clears a foreign pad by the published distance; both presets state what their fab publishes. The cross-crate check sits in `cypcb-cli` beside the mask one, against the constraints table rather than `DesignRules`, because the checker's own view carries no pour clearance - no rule reads one.
- DONE: **the second of the fifteen unread numbers: a hole too near the routed edge.** The board is milled out of a panel and a drilled hole whose wall sits closer to that cut than the fab allows comes out open on one side - a mounting hole with a notch, or a plated hole with no barrel. `min_edge_clearance` cannot answer it: that rule measures **copper**, and a mounting hole has none at all, so a drill with no copper is invisible to it by construction. `HoleToEdgeRule` measures the hole wall - centre plus the drill radius - against the same outline the copper rule uses, through the same `distance_to_outline` rather than a second copy of it.
- **Silent on everything in the repository**, checked before believing it: every `examples/*.cypcb` and all three routed KiCad benchmarks report 0. The rule exists for the board somebody has not written yet, which is what the test fixtures stand in for.
- **The first version of the test could not have shown anything.** It put a 3.2mm hole inside a 3.6mm pad and expected the copper rule to pass while the hole failed - impossible, because a concentric hole is always further from the edge than the copper around it, so the copper rule always fires first. The case that matters is the mounting hole: no copper anywhere, invisible to the copper rule, 0.1mm from the cut.
- The registry is 23 rules. Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test a_hole_the_router_would_break_into` -> 5 passed, including the boundary either side of the published 0.3mm - a via wall at exactly 0.3mm passes, at 0.29mm it does not - and the control well inside the board.
- **`min_pad_size` was implemented, measured, and thrown away - which is the result.** The third of the fifteen unread numbers reads as "the smallest copper pad the fab will etch", and JLCPCB publishes 0.5mm. Written as a rule over every copper pad's narrow side it was silent on all twenty-odd examples and on two of the three routed benchmarks, and then reported **16 pads on `usb_joystick_routed.kicad_pcb`**: `Pad A1 is 0.250mm across its narrow side, 0.500mm required` and fifteen more, all of them J1 - a USB-C connector. JLCPCB builds USB-C boards every day, and its published trace and space is 0.127mm.
- **So the plain reading is refuted by a board that fab manufactures routinely.** `min_pad_size` is not a limit on SMD land width; it is most likely a minimum via land or through-hole pad diameter, where 0.5mm on a 0.3mm drill is the ordinary figure. That is an inference, not a fact this project holds, and a checker that flags every fine-pitch connector is a checker people turn off. The rule and its field were reverted: registry back to 23, `grep -c "pad-size" ...` on that board back to 0.
- **What this cost and what it bought.** One fire, and the discipline held where it matters: the rule was measured against a real board before it shipped rather than after somebody trusted it. The remaining twelve unread numbers are not all like this - `min_hole_to_edge` and `min_paste_clearance` each mapped to exactly one geometry - but the ones whose meaning is ambiguous now have a worked example of how to find out.
- **The gate caught a third flake, and this one had a stated cause.** `a_saved_design_is_checked_again` passes on its own in **0.41s** and failed inside the full gate at **20.02s** - exactly its own deadline, with the rest of the workspace compiling and testing alongside it. Its docstring says it waits for output rather than sleeping "because a test that fails when the machine is busy teaches people to ignore it", and then it did precisely that. The deadline is 60s now, sized for a loaded machine, and the panic says how long it actually waited. A generous deadline costs nothing when the watcher works: the loop returns the moment the log says what it is waiting for.
- **D6, for the owner**: what does `min_pad_size` govern - via lands, through-hole pads, or something else? Until that is answered the number stays unread, deliberately.
- DONE: **two more of the fifteen closed by one rule - `max_drill_aspect_ratio` and `board_thickness`.** Plating a through hole is chemistry rather than machining: copper is pulled down the barrel out of solution, and past some depth-to-width ratio the solution stops refreshing in the middle. The board comes back with a barrel that is thin or open somewhere nobody can see. Every fab publishes the ratio it still plates - 8:1 on JLCPCB's standard process, 12:1 on its advanced one - and nothing read the number.
- **It could not be written before this week.** Aspect ratio is thickness divided by drill, and the checker had no thickness: `stackup` was parsed and dropped. Now that a declared stackup reaches the model, `DrillAspectRatioRule` takes the depth from the design when the design states one and from the fab's own `board_thickness` when it does not - not from a constant typed into the checker.
- **This is the distinction the rule exists for, and a test pins it:** a 0.3mm via is JLCPCB's own minimum drill, so every rule about the drill alone passes it on any board. Through 1.6mm it is 5.3:1 and ordinary; through 3.2mm it is 10.7:1 and unbuildable. `the_drill_rule_says_nothing_about_this_board` asserts 0 `ViaDrill`/`DrillSize` violations on that board and 1 from this rule.
- **Non-plated holes are not asked to plate.** A mounting hole is drilled and left bare, so there is no copper in it to come out thin; the rule skips `PadDef::is_non_plated`, the same question the drill file asks when it decides which file a hole belongs in. A rule without that skip fires on every screw hole in every thick board - which is what the mutation check showed when the skip was removed.
- **Measured across everything in the repository before believing it**: all 21 `examples/*.cypcb`, the three routed KiCad benchmarks and the six benchmark fixtures report **0**. The smallest drill anywhere in the corpus is 0.3mm through 1.6mm, which is 5.3:1. The rule exists for the board nobody has written yet.
- **Proved through the real command, not only in unit tests.** A 20x20 two-layer board declaring `stackup { copper 0.035mm core 3.13mm copper 0.035mm }` with one via: `cypcb check` prints `drill-aspect-ratio at (10.000mm, 10.000mm): via 'SIG': A 0.300mm hole through a 3.20mm board is 10.7:1, more than the 8.0:1 this fab plates - 0.400mm is the smallest that reaches`. The violation carries the drill as `actual` and the smallest drill that would work as `required`, because widening the hole is the fix a person can act on.
- **Mutation checks, both failing the way they should.** Ignoring the design's stackup and always taking the fab's thickness: `the_same_via_passes_on_a_thin_board_and_fails_on_a_thick_one` and `the_drill_rule_says_nothing_about_this_board` fail with `left: 0, right: 1`. Plating the mounting hole: `a_hole_nobody_plates_is_not_asked_to_plate` fails with the H1 message in `left`.
- **A doc comment that had gone false, fixed in the same commit.** `reader.rs`'s `stackup` parser still said "Nothing downstream consumes `BoardDef::stackup`: the checker takes its stackup from the fab preset". Both halves are now wrong - the checker grades the stackup against the layer count and divides by its thickness. Proof the fields have readers: `grep -rn "\bmax_drill_aspect_ratio\b" --include=*.rs crates/ | grep -v "^crates/cypcb-rules/"` -> 9 lines, was 0.
- The registry is 24 rules - `grep -c 'Box::new(rules::' crates/cypcb-drc/src/lib.rs`. Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test a_hole_too_deep_to_plate` -> 6 passed, including the boundary either side of 8:1 through 1.6mm - a 0.2mm hole passes, 0.1999mm does not - and `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- **Ten of the fifteen are still unread**, plus `min_pad_size` held deliberately at D6: `blind_vias_allowed`, `buried_vias_allowed`, `castellated_holes_allowed`, `diff_pair_gap`, `diff_pair_tolerance`, `max_copper_layers`, `max_stub_length`, `max_vias_per_high_speed_net`, `min_acid_trap`, `min_slot_clearance`.
- DONE: **`min_slot_clearance` was pulled and turned into something larger: this tool could not open a board with a slot at all.** Reading it meant finding a slot in the model, and there was none - so the question became what happens to one today. `(pad "2" thru_hole oval ... (drill oval 2.4 1.0))` is what KiCad writes for a slot, and `cypcb check` on such a board said: `Invalid data: pad drill is not a number: String("oval"). A coordinate must be a plain decimal, so (at 105, 80) is one comma away from (at 105 80).` The whole board refused, over a comma that was never there. Every USB connector, barrel jack and latching header holds itself down through a slot.
- **The `.kicad_mod` reader had the opposite defect and the worse one.** It took the drill's width and dismissed the height in a comment - `// Use width as drill diameter (height is for oval drills)` - so a slot imported as a round hole, silently, and every file downstream agreed with it. A slot delivered round is a part that does not fit and a board that is scrap.
- **What shipped**: `PadDef::slot: Option<(Nm, Nm)>` carries the hole's full size exactly as KiCad writes it, `drill` keeps the **narrow** dimension because that is what every rule about a drill means - the bit the fab owns, the width the plating reaches down, the wall a router breaks into. Both readers fill it; the Excellon writer mills it; `to-kicad` writes the oval back. 53 pad literals in 21 files gained the field, and the compiler proved none were missed.
- **The drill file mills it rather than drilling it.** Excellon has one way to order a slot: put the bit down at one end centre and drive it to the other, `X..Y..G85X..Y..`. On the fixture through the real command: `X18.730000Y11.300000G85X18.730000Y12.700000` with tool `T2C1.000000` - a 1mm bit travelling 1.4mm, which is `long - narrow`, on a part rotated 90 degrees so the slot runs along y. Before this the same hole was one point and a 1mm tool: a round hole, ordered from the fab, with nothing in the file saying otherwise.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-kicad --test a_slot_is_not_a_round_hole` -> 5 passed; `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test the_drill_file_mills_a_slot` -> 4 passed; `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`. Mutation checks: taking the long axis as the drill fails `the_drill_is_the_narrow_dimension` with `left: [Some(Nm(2400000))] right: [Some(Nm(1000000))]`; writing the start point alone fails both slot tests in the drill file.
- **A square oval is a round hole.** `(drill oval 1.0 1.0)` is legal KiCad and means a 1mm drill; `PadDef::is_slot` requires the two to differ, so nothing sends a zero-length milling path for a hole one hit makes.
- DONE: **the slot reaches the picture too, so nothing about it is drawn as something else.** The snapshot is the whole of what the browser knows about a board and it carried one drill number per pad - the slot's **narrow** dimension. The engine imported a 2.4x1.0mm slot correctly, milled it correctly into the drill file, and then told the viewer about a 1mm round hole; the renderer drew exactly what it was told. A designer places parts by looking at the board, so a hole drawn at less than half its length is a hole somebody routes a trace across.
- `PadInfo::slot_nm` is `[width, height]` and is **absent** from the JSON for a round hole rather than null, so a snapshot written before slots existed still reads and the common case costs no bytes. The renderer draws the oblong, plating ring included, and a square oval stays a circle in all three places that ask - importer, drill file and screen.
- Proof, through the browser's own path (KiCad text in, snapshot out): `cargo test -p cypcb-render --test a_slot_reaches_the_browser` -> 3 passed, asserting `"slot_nm":[2400000,1000000]`, `"drill_nm":1000000`, and exactly one `slot_nm` on a two-pad footprint. `npx vitest run src/__tests__/a-slot-is-drawn-as-a-slot.test.ts` -> 3 passed: the hole measures 48x20 screen px at 20px/mm, where the drill number alone drew a 20px circle. Mutation: forcing the renderer back to a circle fails with `a slot is not a circle: expected 'circle' to be 'oblong'`.
- DONE: **before `min_slot_clearance` could mean anything, the rules that already ask about holes had to stop treating a slot as a dot.** Every one of them measured a hole as a circle of the pad's drill number, which for a slot is its **narrow** dimension - so a 2.4x1.0mm slot was measured at its centre and was wrong by 0.7mm in the direction it is long, which is exactly the direction the next hole usually is. Two slots with **0.4mm** of laminate between their ends, on a process that publishes 0.5mm, were reported as **1.8mm** apart and passed. The fab breaks through between them and the two holes come out as one.
- A hole is a capsule now - a segment with a radius - and a drilled hole is that same capsule with both ends in one place, so nothing about a round hole changed. `Hole`, `holes_of` and `segment_distance` live in `rules/mod.rs`; the three rules that ask about holes had three copies of the same via-and-pad collection loop and now share one. Net: `hole_to_hole.rs` -99/+~30, `hole_to_edge.rs` -78, `drill_aspect_ratio.rs` -82, against 210 lines of shared geometry that also carries the slot.
- **The closed-form segment distance was written first and was wrong for the only case this exists for.** Two parallel segments leave its denominator at zero and the fallback branch pins one parameter at an endpoint: two slots laid end to end in a row - which is how a connector's two anchors sit - measured 2.8mm apart when their ends were 1.4mm apart, and the new test failed on the new code. Replaced by the smallest of the four endpoint-to-segment distances, with crossing segments answering zero.
- `PadDef::slot_half_travel` moved into `cypcb-world` from the Excellon writer, because the checker needs the same two ends the drill file mills between; one definition, not two.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test a_slot_is_measured_end_to_end` -> 5 passed, including both controls - two slots offset across their length stay silent, and a slot's *depth* is still its narrow dimension because its length is a milling distance. `cargo test -p cypcb-drc` -> 158 + 12 suites, 0 failed, so the refactor changed nothing for round holes. Corpus unchanged at **0** hole-rule violations across all 21 examples, three routed benchmarks, six benchmark fixtures and the slotted fixture. Mutation: measuring from the centres again fails `two_slots_end_to_end_are_as_close_as_their_ends` with `left: 0, right: 1`. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- **`min_slot_clearance` was read against the fab's own page rather than guessed, and it does not settle - so it is D7 and stays unread.** JLCPCB's published capability table has no slot clearance figure of any kind. What it does publish about slots: `Min. Plated Slots Width` 0.5mm two-layer and 0.35mm multi-layer, `Min. Non-Plated Slots` 1.0mm, a slot size tolerance, and 0.2mm of copper clearance from a routed edge. Read literally the way the field's own doc comment says - copper to slot - the rule fires on every slotted pad ever drawn, because a plated slot has its own annulus around it by construction. That is the shape of trap `min_pad_size` turned out to be, and the answer this time was one page-read rather than an implement-measure-revert.
- **Found while reading it, not fixed: no preset table carries a minimum slot width.** JLCPCB will not mill a plated slot under 0.5mm and `min_drill_size` is 0.3mm, so a 0.4mm slot passes `cypcb check` today and cannot be made. Filling that in means reading five fabs' tables rather than one, which is owner-scale research and not something to infer from the one page read here.
- DONE: **the multiplication that turns a pad's offset into a board coordinate existed five times, and two copies had already drifted.** Two in `cypcb-autoroute`, one in `cypcb-drc`, two in `cypcb-export` - and the copper writer **truncated** the rotated offset toward zero where the drill writer **rounded** it, so the same pad's flash and its own hole could land a nanometre apart, asymmetrically about the origin. Nothing caught it because every bundled board is placed at a multiple of 90 degrees, where the trigonometry lands on whole nanometres and the two agree exactly.
- One definition now: `cypcb_world::components::place_pad` and `rotate_about_origin`, beside the pads they place. It rounds, because truncation is a bias rather than a rounding rule.
- **Before and after on the real files: zero geometry lines change.** Exported `blink`, `four-layer` and `cutout` at `bf61a0c` and again with the change: 38 files differ and **every one of them differs only in its `CreationDate`** - `diff -r | grep -E "^[<>]" | grep -vc "CreationDate|export_date"` -> **0**. The drift was real and latent, not live.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-export --test one_pad_one_place` -> 2 passed - a part at 45 degrees, where a 1mm offset lands on 707106.78nm, and both files write `10.707107`. `cargo test --workspace --exclude cypcb-desktop` -> 0 failures. Mutation: putting truncation back in the shared helper fails both. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **the language can ask for a slot, so it stopped being an import-only feature.** A slot reached the model, the drill file, the KiCad file and the screen, and the one place it could not come from was a `.cypcb` file - `sync.rs` wrote `slot: None` with a comment saying the language had no way to say it. `drill 2.4mm x 1.0mm` says it now, written the way `size W x H` is because it is the same question asked of the hole rather than of the copper. One number is still a round hole, so nothing about an existing design changes.
- **Both readers, not one.** `node_modules/.bin/tree-sitter` is in the grammar directory after all, so `drill_spec` gained `field('width')` and an optional `x field('height')` and the generated parser was rebuilt - the differential test reads every example both ways and is the proof they agree. It also caught the mistake: an rsync pushed the stale local `parser.c` over the regenerated one, tree-sitter returned `drill: null` for **every** pad, and the test failed with both ASTs printed side by side.
- `examples/slotted-connector.cypcb` is the board: a USB receptacle's two shell anchors as `drill 2.4mm x 1.0mm` beside two ordinary 0.9mm pins, every pad on a net and reached. `cypcb check` -> `OK ... passed DRC`, rc=0. Its drill file carries `T1C1.000000` with `X10.300000Y6.000000G85X11.700000Y6.000000` and its twin - a 1mm bit travelling 1.4mm - and `T2C0.900000` with two plain hits.
- **A corpus guard failed on it and the guard was the thing that was wrong.** `every_example_reaches_the_files` looks for each pad's hole at the pad's own centre, and read only the first coordinate pair of a line - so a milled slot landed half its own length away and it reported `no hole at (11.000mm, 6.000mm)`. It reads both ends of a `G85` and takes their midpoint now, which is where the pad is.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-world --test a_design_can_ask_for_a_slot` -> 4 passed, including a slot written tall - the pair is stored as written rather than sorted, because which way the hole runs is what the drill mills along - and `drill 1.0mm x 1.0mm` staying a round hole. `cargo test -p cypcb-parser --features tree-sitter-parser --test differential` -> 3 passed. Mutation: dropping the second dimension in `sync.rs` fails both slot tests with `right: Some((Nm(2400000), Nm(1000000)))`. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- DONE: **the editor said a slot was a round hole, and hovering your own footprint said nothing at all.** Two surfaces, one fire. The language server's hover card lists each pad as `shape W x H, drill D`, and for a slot `D` is the **narrow** dimension - so a 2.4x1.0mm anchor read as `drill 1.00mm`, a round hole under half the length of the one the part needs, stated with the same confidence as every other number on the card. It says `slot 2.4mm x 1mm` now.

A designer got less about their own footprint than about a part they did not write. It lists them now, under the same eight-pad limit the built-in card uses so a QFP does not bury the screen.
- The viewer's editor gained two completions - a through-hole pad and a slotted one - and hover text for `pad` and `drill` that names both forms. `docs/SYNTAX.md` carries the grammar line `[drill <d> [x <d2>]]` and a section on drilled against milled holes, pointing at `examples/slotted-connector.cypcb`.

So both halves of KiCad interoperation had only ever been checked against this project's own idea of the format.

The numbers live in the `.kicad_pro` beside the board under `board.design_settings.rules`, read out of KiCad's own template and demo projects. Measured with `kicad-cli pcb drc` on routing-test routed in-house: without a project file 8 `track_width` and 1 `clearance` against KiCad's own 0.2mm, with one 0 and 0 against JLCPCB's published 0.127mm.

- **Past the gate, a KiCad 10 board read as having no nets at all.** KiCad 10 dropped the numbered net table every version since 5 carried and writes the name alone: `(net "VBUS")`, not `(net 3 "VBUS")`. `net_count: 0` on all three boards tested. `NetIndex` resolves either spelling, and the name walk runs only when there is no table - a two-element `(net 1)` is a number on every older board and on everything this project writes, and reading it as a name interns a net called "1" per segment. That is what the first attempt did, and an existing round-trip test caught it.
- `crates/cypcb-kicad/tests/fixtures/kicad10-slotted.kicad_pcb` is the first file here KiCad wrote, 19 uuids, guarded by a test against being replaced by another hand-written one.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-kicad --test a_board_kicad_actually_wrote` -> 4 passed. `cargo test -p cypcb-cli --test the_kicad_board_carries_the_rules_it_was_checked_with` -> 7 passed. Mutation, restoring the `(rules ...)` node: `pcbnew will not open a board with this in it`. `cypcb parse-kicad` on the three boards KiCad saved -> 7, 3 and 2 nets, which is what the three designs declare.
- **Still open, and not a fault of the same kind: no 3D models.** The writer emits no `(model ...)` line, and shipping one means a table mapping this project's footprint names to KiCad's - `0402` to `Resistor_SMD.3dshapes/R_0402_1005Metric.wrl` - where a wrong entry silently shows the wrong part. Nothing on this machine can verify such a table either: `kicad-packages3d` is not installed and `/usr/share/kicad/3dmodels` is empty, and the package is 3.1 GiB. Owner-scale decision, not a fire.
- DONE: **`cypcb from-kicad` - a KiCad board comes out as text somebody can edit.** `to-kicad` had shipped and the other direction did not exist: a KiCad board could be checked, routed, scored and exported here, and nothing turned it into `.cypcb` source, so the one thing this project is for was the one thing a KiCad user could not get out of it. The whole DSL writer was `traces_as_dsl` and it wrote traces; there was no way to write a board, an outline, a component, a net or a footprint. `board_as_dsl` writes all of them.
- Measured on the six benchmark boards, component and net counts identical to what `parse-kicad` reads out of the originals: led_blink 7/7, stm32_breakout 29/40, multi_ic 52/94, shift_driver 55/55, qfp_fanout 19/50, plane_board 12/15. Four of the six make the whole trip - board in, `.cypcb` out, `to-kicad` back - with component count, net count, layer count and board size unchanged, and a slot survives it as a slot.
- Three decisions taken rather than guessed. **What a part is**: KiCad never records it, so the kind comes from the reference designator prefix - R, C, L, U, D, Q, J, Y, the convention every schematic has used - and `generic`, which the language has for exactly this, where the prefix is not one of them. Deriving a kind from the footprint name would be inventing a fact about the board. **What a footprint is called**: `cypcb:USB_ANCHOR` becomes a bare identifier, collisions are numbered rather than merged, and a test checks that every component names exactly what was defined. **What cannot be written**: a copper pour has no syntax, so a board carrying one gets a comment saying how many were dropped rather than losing them quietly.
- **Found by it, and open: the language cannot name a pad.** `pad_definition` takes a *number*, and a USB-C receptacle's pads are called A1, A4, A5, A6, A7, B1, B4, S1, S2 - two rows and a shell, on every USB-C part there is. Two of the six boards carry one, and `from-kicad` re-reads what it wrote, so it catches this and says what happened instead of writing a file that will not parse. Renaming them would move pins onto the wrong nets, so it does not.

In memory every segment a net has on a layer lives in one `Trace` entity, and `ClearanceRule` reports once per entity pair with the closest distance it found, so a component too close to a net **in two places is reported once**. - **The new rule found a defect in the geometry it depends on.** `segment_distance`'s degenerate-first-segment branch computed `t = f/e` where the maths gives `-f/e`, which walks the closest point to the wrong end of the segment. The general branch computes `(b*s - f)/e` - the same thing with the right sign - so the two disagreed. Nothing had exercised it: its only caller, `point_to_segment_distance`, carried `#[allow(dead_code)]`. Silkscreen violations were silently under-reported until it was fixed, and a regression test now pins the perpendicular case, the past-the-end case and argument symmetry.

The requirement for a pair is now the strictest thing either side asked for, never below the fab floor. Two things had to change with it: the broad phase expanded its query by the preset, so a pair needing more space was filtered out before anyone could ask what it required; and the net set was read from entities carrying a `NetId`, which misses a board with no traces yet, so it comes from the net registry now. Proven on one board, twice: clean under the preset, and `R1 ↔ R2: 0.30mm actual, 0.60mm required` once HV states 0.6mm.
- DONE: **clearance is a copper rule, and it was being measured against part bodies.** A component sits in the spatial index as its footprint's **courtyard** - the assembly keepout over the whole body - and `ClearanceRule` measured traces against that box. So a trace running through the 0.4mm gap between a 0402's two pads, which every real board does, was reported as a dead short at 0.00mm. The narrow phase now resolves a component to its pad copper, the way it already resolved a trace to its segments, and honours each pad's own layers: a bottom-layer trace cannot short a pad that only exists on top. Two failures came out of the same investigation. `CourtyardClearanceRule` - the rule that is *supposed* to own body collisions - filtered the spatial index for `layer_mask == 0`, and no index builder in the crate sets that (components are indexed `0xFFFFFFFF`), so it silently reported zero on every board ever checked; it reads the components directly now. And `parse_kicad_pcb` never called `set_footprints`, so on an imported board the world held no footprints at all and every rule that needs pad or silk geometry quietly degraded. Measured with `drc_report`, before / after: stm32_breakout **173 -> 124 introduced** (clearance 152 -> 103), multi_ic **122 -> 42** (clearance 108 -> 28), led_blink 0 -> 0. The pre-routing baselines rose the other way as the blind rules woke up - multi_ic 5 -> 60, of which 23 courtyard-clearance, 20 solder-mask-bridge and 19 silk-clearance were always true of that fixture and never once reported. Workspace: 52 targets, 1315 passed, 0 failed.

Exactly the defect the CI regression gate was fixed for in this vector, one layer up. `VariantResult.unrouted` is carried now and the sort is complete-first, then fewer abandoned, then composite.
