- `variant_picks_per_board` asserts `winner.unrouted == 0` before it compares scores, and prints the count per row so a ranking cannot hide one again.
- **led_blink's four, printed rather than guessed.** `drc_report` runs both settings now. Default: one short at 0.00mm and one gap at 0.08mm. Reserved copper: 0.02mm, 0.02mm, 0.10mm and 0.05mm - no shorts, four near misses. Two of them are the same pair at the same coordinate with the same message, which is a duplicate the checker emits, not two faults on the board.
- DONE: **the checker counted one gap twice, and the boards were 8% and 13% cleaner than every score in this project said.** Where a trace bends and the corner is the nearest point to the other feature, both segments meeting there reported it - the same coordinate, the same message, twice. Per-segment reporting exists so a trace violating in three places counts three; one place counted twice is not that. Contacts are now keyed by point with the worst distance kept, and sorted so the list does not reshuffle run to run. Measured, same routing on all three: stm32_breakout **259 -> 239** introduced, multi_ic **143 -> 124**, led_blink unchanged at 2, and under reserved copper led_blink 4 -> 3. Ratchets lowered with it - `DRC_RATCHETS` 271 -> 251 and 210 -> 191 - with a note saying the router did not improve, the checker stopped double-counting.
- The unit test bends a trace over a pad corner and asserts one violation; on the previous commit it reports two at `(0.5, 1.05)` with an identical message.
- DONE: **the trace-to-trace half of that shape is covered, checked rather than assumed.** `per_segment_to_trace` pairs every segment of one trace against every segment of the other, so two bends facing each other can find the same corner from several pairs. Two traces whose corners sit 0.2mm apart now have a test: it passes on the dedupe and reports the gap **twice at (0.5, 1.1) with an identical message** when the dedupe is taken out, which is what makes it a guard rather than a decoration.
- DONE: **the reservation yields instead of vetoing, and stm32_breakout picks it now.** Copper a trace merely brushes is marked `CELL_HALO` rather than `CELL_TRACE`, and a net that finds no path at all gets a second attempt that may route through halo cells - never through another net's centre line, which is a short. An abandoned connection is a board that does not work; a tight gap is a violation the checker names. Fourth attempt at a hard block in this vector and the first that pays, because it is the first that can be relaxed.

| board | winner before | winner now |
|---|---|---|
| stm32_breakout | `Low-Via` 261,564.3 / 224 violations / 0 unrouted | **`Reserved Copper` 195,100.7 / 180 / 0 unrouted** |
| multi_ic | `Reserved Copper` 133,611.1 / 128 | unchanged |
| led_blink | `High-Density` 42.6 / 0 | unchanged, `Reserved Copper` 3rd-from-last at 3 |

- Measured on the routing itself, `drc_report`: stm32_breakout under reserved copper goes from `Partial { unrouted_count: 3 }` with 137 introduced to **`Complete` with 168**, against the default path's 239. Two of the three boards now pick the variant that reserves copper, and both are complete.
- DONE: **a violation carries the distance it measured, and a short is no longer the same thing as a tight gap.** `DrcViolation` held its numbers only inside a formatted sentence, so anything ranking violations had to parse English or treat 0.00mm and 0.05mm as equal - copper touching copper and a gap under spec, a board that cannot work and a board a fab may still build. `actual` and `required` are fields now, `RoutingScore.shorts` counts the touching ones, and variant ranking is complete-first, then fewer shorts, then composite.
- **What that reveals is the real case for reserving copper: it halves the shorts.** stm32_breakout 159 shorts under the default against **82** under `Reserved Copper`; multi_ic 75 against **29**; led_blink 1 against **0**. The violation totals had been hiding it, because a reservation trades shorts for near misses and the composite charges both 1000.
- led_blink re-ranks accordingly: `Reserved Copper` moves from fifth to **second**, ahead of `PathFinder Default` - 3 violations and no shorts beats 2 violations one of which is copper on copper. `PathFinder High-Density` still wins it outright at 0 and 0.
- `variants_sorted_by_composite_score` is renamed and rewritten to the real contract; the JSON shape test moved 7 fields to 8 and names why.

Run on `examples/drc-test.cypcb` and `examples/blink.cypcb --in-house`, output above quoted from those runs.

A gap under spec is a yield risk, not permission to ship - the split says what the board has, and the CLI test asserts both halves: the line appears, and the command still exits non-zero.

Turning `reserve_trace_footprint` on as the default and running the gate:

| fixture | violations | shorts | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| led_blink | 3 against 2 | **0 against 1** | fails the violation column |
| stm32_breakout | **180 against 251** | **82 against 159** | passes both, by a distance |
| multi_ic | **128 against 191** | **29 against 75** | passes both, by a distance |

- **Decision: the default stays off, and the ratchet stays at 2.** Raising a ratchet because the router changed is the thing this file forbids, and led_blink is the one board where the setting costs something. What it costs is one short traded for two near misses at 0.02mm and 0.10mm - better by severity, worse by count - and that is an argument, not a measurement. The setting keeps winning both dense boards through `--variants`, which is what the mechanism is for.
- DONE: **read led_blink net by net, and its extra violation has a name.** `what_the_reservation_costs_led_blink` routes the board both ways and prints the breakdown. Under the reservation **GND stops being a top-layer net**: 14 segments and no vias become 11 segments and **3 vias** onto the bottom layer, at exactly the same 39.0mm of copper, and SW_OUT gives up the via it had. One of GND's new vias lands 0.05mm from SW_OUT - that is the third violation, and the other two are the same C1 pair the default has, at **0.02mm and 0.10mm against the default's 0.00mm and 0.08mm**. The reservation makes both of the shared ones better and adds one of its own.
- **Failed experiment, measured, reverted: refusing a via whose keepout holds foreign copper.** The diagnosis points straight at it - a via is far more copper than the cell the path walks, and the trace radius cannot cover a ring. It works on the board it was aimed at and wrecks the others: led_blink 3 violations -> **2**, 0 shorts; stm32_breakout 180 -> 215; multi_ic **128 -> 245** violations and **29 -> 111** shorts. The first cut also left stm32_breakout 2 connections unrouted until the fallback attempt was allowed to yield the via room as well. Reverted, and the revert re-measured the ratchets back to 2/1, 251/159 and 191/75 exactly. Fifth measurement in this vector saying a veto during expansion costs more than it buys.
- DONE: **the price worked where five vetoes failed, and the default moved.** `via_foreign_copper_penalty` charges a via for each foreign cell inside the keepout its ring needs, instead of forbidding the via. At 2.0 it repeated the veto's shape - stm32_breakout 159 violations but multi_ic 231 - and at **0.5** every fixture improved on both columns at once. `reserve_trace_footprint` and the price are the default now:

| fixture | before (violations / shorts) | after |
|---|---|---|
| led_blink | 2 / 1 | **2 / 0** |
| stm32_breakout | 251 / 159 | **171 / 91** |
| multi_ic | 191 / 75 | **154 / 54** |

- Ratchets lowered to the measured values on both columns, which is the first time in this vector they have moved because the router got better rather than because the checker changed.
- **A gate that measured the wrong thing went with it.** `benchmark_regression` asserted `route_count >= 20` as a stand-in for "the router did not give up" - a job the `unrouted == 0` assertion already does. It tripped when the same board came out in 18 segments instead of 23 with the same 79mm of copper: fewer corners is better. It asserts copper length now.
- The variant set follows the default rather than opting out of it, and `PathFinder Reserved Copper` is replaced by `PathFinder Bare Centre Line` - the router as it was, kept as the control. Best-of-six after the change: led_blink `High-Density` 0/0, stm32_breakout `Low-Via` **158 / 74**, multi_ic `Guarded Pads` **118 / 26**, all better than the best any board could reach before this fire.
- DONE: **swept the price instead of keeping the first number that worked, and the first number was the wrong one.** `via_price_sweep` routes all three fixtures at 0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0. Introduced violations and shorts:

| price | led_blink | stm32_breakout | multi_ic | total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00 | 3 / 0 | 168 / 82 | **61 / 29** | 232 / 111 |
| **0.25** | 2 / 0 | **121 / 58** | 73 / 37 | **196 / 95** |
| 0.50 | 2 / 0 | 159 / 91 | 87 / 54 | 248 / 145 |
| 1.00 | 2 / 0 | 138 / 76 | 109 / 59 | 249 / 135 |
| 2.00 | 2 / 0 | 147 / 84 | 164 / 105 | 313 / 189 |

- **The response is not monotone and the boards do not agree**, which is the reason to sweep rather than reason. multi_ic is happiest at zero and gets worse with every increase; stm32_breakout has a floor at 0.25 and rises on both sides of it; led_blink needs any price above zero to stop putting a via 0.05mm from a foreign trace. 0.25 is the point that costs multi_ic 12 violations to save stm32_breakout 47.
- Default moved 0.5 -> 0.25 and the ratchets with it: stm32_breakout **171/91 -> 133/58**, multi_ic **154/54 -> 140/37**, led_blink unchanged at 2/0. The 0.5 that shipped last fire was measured on two points and beaten by a third.
- DONE: **measured the noise floor, and it is as wide as the tuning this vector has been doing.** Prices a hair apart ask the router for the same trade, so what they differ by is what negotiated congestion does on its own. `how_much_of_the_price_is_noise` routes the dense fixtures at 0.22, 0.24, 0.25, 0.26 and 0.28:

| price | stm32_breakout | multi_ic |
|---|---|---|
| 0.22 | 145 / 74 | 92 / 54 |
| 0.24 | 126 / 63 | 77 / 42 |
| 0.25 | 121 / 58 | 73 / 37 |
| 0.26 | 149 / 81 | 61 / 28 |
| 0.28 | 138 / 66 | 75 / 44 |
| **spread** | **28 violations** | **31 violations** |

- **That is the same size as the differences the sweep was choosing between.** 0.25 against 0.5 was 38 violations on stm32_breakout, barely outside a band of 28 that a hundredth of a price can produce. The seven knobs measured earlier in this vector, and the price picked last fire, were fitted to runs inside their own noise. The default stays at 0.25 - it is not shown to be better than 0.24, and it is not worse either.
- **The ratchets carry that band now, and it is not slack.** A threshold set to one measured run fails on any unrelated change that only perturbs rip-up ordering, which is a gate that cries wolf. Each dense fixture is allowed its measured value plus the spread measured beside it: stm32_breakout 133/58 -> thresholds 161/81, multi_ic 140/37 -> 171/63. led_blink has no band - it returned 2/0 at every price above zero.
- **Failed experiment, measured, reverted: best of several net orderings.** The plan was to turn the 28-violation band into a floor - route N times with the order rotated, keep the best, the way `--variants` keeps the best of six configs. Built it (`attempts`, `net_order_rotation`, and an apply-score-clear helper shared with the variant path) and it bought **nothing**: stm32_breakout 121 introduced at 1, 3 and 5 attempts, multi_ic 73 at all three, led_blink 2 - identical results at three and five times the wall clock.
- **The reason is that the premise was wrong, and the knob proves it.** Rotating the order is not a neutral shuffle: `order_nets` puts short nets first and power last for a reason, so every rotation is worse and the best-of always returns the unrotated one. Measured directly - one step of rotation takes stm32_breakout from **133/58 to 149/65** and led_blink from 18 segments to 19. The band between neighbouring prices therefore does not come from order sensitivity as written here; it comes from the negotiation trajectory itself, where a cost change of a hundredth sends rip-up down a different path.
- DONE: **printed the negotiation trajectory, and it says the router never converges on either dense board.** `PathFinderLoopResult` carries the overused count per iteration now, and `where_the_band_comes_from` prints it at two prices a hundredth apart:

```
stm32_breakout  0.24: 12 iterations, converged false, [695, 514, 340, 361, 377, 336, 297, 284, 289, 319, 304]
stm32_breakout  0.26:  7 iterations, converged false, [673, 495, 320, 348, 346, 365]
multi_ic        0.24:  9 iterations, converged false, [538, 364, 268, 271, 256, 273, 285, 318]
multi_ic        0.26: 13 iterations, converged false, [553, 339, 269, 270, 258, 278, 270, 257, 237, 256, 262, 258]
```

- **Three facts, none of them the ramp.** The runs differ from iteration 1, so the price changes the first routing and everything after is a different trajectory - not an accident late in a schedule. Overuse **oscillates** rather than descending: 340, 361, 377, 336, 297, 284, 289, 319, 304. And both boards stop on the stagnation break with 250-380 cells still shared between two nets, so a run's length - 7 against 12 - is decided by where an oscillating series happened to be when a "no progress for three iterations" test looked at it. That is the band.
- **Failed experiment, measured, reverted: returning the iteration with the fewest overused cells instead of the last one.** It is the obvious read of the oscillation and it made both dense boards worse - stm32_breakout **133 -> 152** violations and 58 -> 69 shorts, multi_ic **140 -> 174** and 37 -> 69. Reverted, and the revert re-measured 133/58 and 140/37 exactly. What it proves is worth more than the change would have been: **the loop's own progress metric does not track the thing the project measures.** Fewer cells shared is not fewer violations, so every stagnation decision in this loop is being made on a proxy nobody has checked.
- DONE: **checked the proxy against the thing it stands for, one iteration at a time.** `max_ripup_iterations` had been on `AutorouteConfig` since the beginning and **only the legacy orchestrator read it** - PathFinder ran to a private constant of 50, so the 10 it defaulted to never applied to the router that ships. Wired up (zero means the strategy's cap, so nothing changed: the gate re-measured 133/58 and 140/37), it makes the loop stoppable at any iteration, which is what the question needed. stm32_breakout at price 0.25, one run per cap:

| cap | overuse entering | introduced | shorts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 694 | 286 | 170 |
| 4 | 380 | 148 | 84 |
| 7 | 296 | 125 | 61 |
| 8 | 298 | 145 | 76 |
| 10 | 324 | 125 | 60 |
| 11 | **460** | **120** | **57** |
| 12 | 332 | 121 | 58 |

- **The proxy is sound early and inverted exactly where the stop decision is made.** Through the first seven iterations overuse and violations fall together, 694/286 to 296/125. In the tail they disagree on every step: the board with the fewest violations of any iteration, 120, is the one the loop saw with **460 overused cells** - its worst reading. The stagnation break is reading a signal that has stopped meaning anything by the time it fires.
- **It costs about one violation, which is why this line of work stops here.** The tail is flat - 125, 145, 140, 125, 120, 121 - so stopping at the wrong point in it is worth a violation or two against a band of 28. Rewiring the stop rule to run DRC per iteration would double the routing time to buy that. Measured and declined.
- **Where the leverage actually is: the first four iterations, 286 -> 148.** Half the violations of a finished board are gone by iteration 4, and every trajectory this vector has printed diverges at iteration 1. The tail has had four fires; the head has had none.
- **Failed experiment, measured, reverted: seeding the congestion map from the ratsnest.** The reasoning was the best this vector had - the first pass runs against an empty map, so every net takes the cheapest corridor as though it were alone, and half a finished board's violations are already decided by iteration 4. Pricing each cell by how many nets' straight lines cross it, before anyone routes, made both dense boards worse at every weight:

| seed | led_blink | stm32_breakout | multi_ic |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.00 | 2 / 0 | **121 / 58** | **73 / 37** |
| 0.25 | 2 / 0 | 142 / 76 | 112 / 70 |
| 0.50 | 2 / 0 | 144 / 75 | 99 / 62 |
| 1.00 | 2 / 0 | 145 / 70 | 87 / 45 |

- The shape of the loss says why: multi_ic goes from 706 segments to 1188 at the lightest seed. Pricing a corridor before anyone has taken it pushes every net off the direct line at once - including the nets that would have got it and been fine - so the first routing is worse and the negotiation spends its iterations recovering. The empty map is not blindness, it is letting the first-come net take the cheap line and charging the rest for what it actually took.
- Reverted, and the revert re-measured 133/58 and 140/37 exactly. That is now **seven instruments measured and dropped in this vector** - four vetoes, best-of-N orderings, best-iteration selection, and this. The two that paid, reserving trace copper and pricing a crowded via, both worked by charging for copper that exists rather than for copper somebody might want.
- DONE: **`docs/routing.md` - the vector's memory, written down.** What PathFinder does and where each piece lives; the two settings that pay with the sweep that chose the price; the noise band and why the ratchets carry it; the trajectory facts that bound what is worth trying (never converges, diverges at iteration 1, overuse inverted in the tail); and a table of **nine instruments measured and dropped**, each with the numbers that killed it. Every claim carries the command that produces it and the file ends with a verification section. Linked from the README beside the architecture doc.
- The pattern the table makes is the useful part: **pricing copper that exists pays, blocking or pricing space somebody might want does not.** Both shipped settings do the first; all nine failures do the second.

- DONE: **the sweep was re-run rather than the table re-typed, and it says something new.** `via_price_sweep` on all three fixtures after the via fix: **zero is now the worst price on every board** (led_blink 4/1, stm32_breakout 265/129, multi_ic 272/173 introduced/shorts). Before the fix multi_ic was happiest at zero and the shipped 0.25 was a compromise between boards that disagreed; the disagreement is gone, which is the expected shape - a price on a via only bites once the via survives to the output. **The shipped value still stays at 0.25**: 1.00 reads 16 violations better on stm32_breakout and 10 on multi_ic, both inside the re-measured noise bands of 38 and 30. A knob is not re-tuned on a difference the router makes on its own.
- DONE: **named the three numbers this project calls "violations", after two of them turned out to be different.** The gate's ratchets hold `violation_count()` on the routed board - **after**; the sweeps and this tracker print **introduced**, matched fault by fault against the fixture's own. stm32_breakout is 144 before, 239 after, 221 introduced; multi_ic 289 / 336 / 247; led_blink 12 / 2 / 2. Introduced is not after minus before, because routing retires faults too - every unrouted pin the fixture starts with is a violation a successful route removes. Measured with `drc_report`, which prints all three and the kinds behind them, and the doc now defines them before it uses them.
- NEXT-ACTION: none in this vector. `docs/routing.md` carries the current tables, the pad veto as the tenth dropped instrument, the three variants, and a dated note on the one section still quoting pre-via-fix counts (the per-iteration trajectory, where only the shape is claimed).
- DONE: **the `--all-targets` lint found another test that could not fail, and the constant it was guarding was wrong.** `assert!(DesignConstraints::FIELD_COUNT >= 30)` compares two literals, so it holds whatever the struct does - and `FIELD_COUNT` said 35 while the struct had 34. The test destructures `DesignConstraints` without `..` now, which makes the compiler refuse to build until every field is named, and asserts that count against the constant. It earned its place immediately: the first version of the list was written from a grep and the compiler rejected it with `pattern does not mention fields default_impedance_ohms_x100, max_current_per_width_x100, copper_weight_oz_x10`. The `cypcb-parser` `map_or` lint is fixed with it. `cargo clippy -p cypcb-rules -p cypcb-parser --all-targets -- -D warnings` -> Finished.
- ~~QUEUED: decide whether the gate should run clippy with `--all-targets`~~ **Decided and done, and this line outlived it.** `scripts/quality-gate.sh:27` runs `cargo clippy --workspace --exclude cypcb-desktop --all-targets -- -D warnings`, so test code is linted by the gate and not only by hand. The seven `unused_mut` are gone too: `cargo clippy -p cypcb-autoroute --all-targets` reports **0**.
- DONE: **the same-net exemption is per pad now, and it was blind in a way no benchmark would have shown.** It exempted a pair as soon as the component carried the trace's net anywhere, so a trace on `GND` crossing the `VCC` pad of a part with one GND pin was silently legal - a dead short the checker was built to catch. Each pad carries its own net now, matched from `PadDef::number` to `PinConnection::pin`, and the exemption is decided per pad inside the narrow phase; component-to-component pairs skip only the pad pairs that share a net. Proven both ways on the same fixture: the new test fails on the previous commit (`git stash push crates/cypcb-drc/src/rules/clearance.rs` -> `a_net_a_part_carries_does_not_exempt_that_part_s_other_pads ... FAILED`) and passes on this one, while `a_trace_meeting_the_pad_it_belongs_to_is_still_exempt` holds throughout - a checker that reports a trace reaching its own pad is unusable. This closes the second half of K010.
- DONE: **measured what the per-pad exemption costs, and it found a real short on the smallest board.** Introduced violations went stm32_breakout **124 -> 174**, multi_ic **42 -> 79**, led_blink **0 -> 1**. Every one of those was already on the board; the checker had been excusing them. led_blink's is worth naming because it is one line: `C1 ↔ trace 'GND': 0.00mm actual` - and the fixture's own netlist puts C1 pad 1 on `SW_OUT`, pad 2 on `GND`, so a GND trace is lying across the switch output. That board does not blink.
- **The mechanism is found and it is not the grid.** `pad_to_zone` builds a disc around every pad of the net being routed - pad radius plus a hard-coded 3 cells, about 0.76mm at this resolution - and inside that disc `find_path_congestion_augmented` accepts a cell whether or not it is an obstacle. The escape hatch exists so a route can reach its own pad through the pad's own keepout. It does not distinguish the target pad from the part's other pads, so a GND route arriving at C1 pad 2 may drive straight over C1 pad 1 on the way in.
- **Two ratchets moved, both upward, both with the reason written at the assertion.** `smoother_integration_led_blink` from `== 0` to `<= 1`, and `benchmark_regression` from `drc_violations == 0` to `<= 1` with composite from 100.0 to 1100.0 (the composite charges 1000 per violation, so 42.6 of quality plus one short). Raising a ratchet is normally forbidden and this is the exception that proves it: the board is unchanged, the checker stopped being blind. Both comments say to put them back the moment the router stops driving through sibling pads.
- **Pad-zone ownership: built, measured in six variants, reverted. The trade is real and it is the owner's to make.** Giving pad cells their net (`PadDef::number` matched to `PinConnection::pin`) and refusing a foreign pad's cells inside the escape hatch does exactly what it was meant to: led_blink's `C1 ↔ trace 'GND'` short disappears and stm32_breakout's introduced violations fall by up to a third. It also costs **exactly 6 unrouted connections on stm32_breakout, in every variant tried**, which is what makes it a decision rather than a fix - the gate asserts `unrouted == 0` first, on the grounds that every quality metric improves when the router gives up.

| variant | stm32 | multi_ic | led_blink | complete |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline, no ownership | 174 | 79 | 1 | yes |
| own pad + clearance, first claim wins | 139 | 69 | 0 | **no, 6 unrouted** |
| own copper only, first claim wins | 142 | 90 | 1 | **no, 6 unrouted** |
| own pad + clearance, contested cells shared | 189 | 84 | 1 | yes |
| rectangular pads + shared | 169 | 83 | 1 | yes |
| rectangular pads + first claim wins | 128 | 67 | 0 | **no, 6 unrouted** |
| rectangular pads, copper only, first claim | 107 | 85 | 0 | **no, 6 unrouted** |
| rectangular pads, no ownership | 177 | 86 | 1 | yes |

  Two things fall out of the table. Ownership is what fixes the short - every variant that keeps a single owner per cell reaches 0 on led_blink, every variant that shares contested cells stays at 1. And the 6 unrouted connections do not move: not with the ring, not without it, not with corrected pad geometry, so they are not a corridor-width problem and the next step is to find out which 6 nets they are and what they cannot get past. Reverted to baseline, which the re-measurement confirms at 174 / 79 / 1, all complete.
- **K011's remaining violation was fixed and it did not pay on its own.** `populate_pads` marking every pad as a circle of `max(w, h) / 2` is wrong - a 1.5mm x 0.6mm pad becomes 0.75mm in every direction - and replacing it with the rotated rectangle, on its own, moved stm32_breakout from 174 to 177 and multi_ic from 79 to 86. The circle was over-conservative in the short axis and that slack was doing useful work. Correct geometry is only worth landing together with the ownership rule it enables, so it went back with it.
- DONE: **the abandoned connections have names now, and they say what the problem is.** The router logged nothing when it gave up, so `Partial { unrouted_count: 6 }` was a number nobody could act on; it names each one through `tracing` now, and `tests/abandoned_connections.rs` turns the subscriber on. Under pad ownership the casualties are almost all escapes from the QFP's pad column - `PA4.6 at 30.750,31.750mm -> PA4.7 at 5.000,65.240mm`, and the same shape for PA5, PA6, PA7, PB4, PB7, I2C_SDA, I2C_SCL - plus two that settle it: `VCC_3V3.12 -> VCC_3V3.20`, 5mm apart across the same pad row, and `GND.48 at 32.250,27.750mm -> GND.46 at 33.250,27.750mm`, **two pads of the same net 1.0mm apart that cannot be connected**. The pins sit on a 0.5mm pitch and a cell is 0.254mm, so the corridor between two pads is one cell wide at best. This is a fan-out problem, not a routing-rule problem: nothing that reasons in whole cells will get a track out of that part.
- **Two more variants measured, both rejected.** Refusing foreign pad copper geometrically per net rather than through a grid ownership map, which removes the first-claim lockout entirely: stm32_breakout **8 unrouted / 94 introduced**, multi_ic **49** (the best figure any variant has produced), led_blink still 1. And rounding the pad core radius **down** instead of up, on the theory that ceil closes the one-cell corridor from both sides: stm32 still 8 unrouted, 120 introduced. The eight do not move for any of it, which is the same signal the six gave - the blocker is the pitch, not the rule.
- **The router does not converge, and nothing said so until the log was turned on.** `PathFinder did not converge within iteration cap: iterations=9 remaining_overuse=363` on stm32_breakout, `iterations=17 remaining_overuse=229` on multi_ic. An overused cell is two nets sharing one cell of copper, so the router is knowingly shipping hundreds of overlaps - which is a far better explanation for the ~147 clearance violations than any pad geometry, and it has been sitting in a warning nobody read.
- **Non-convergence is not the cause either, and the shipped stagnation limit is the right one.** The correspondence between 363 overused cells and 147 clearance violations was suggestive and wrong. `stagnation_limit` is a config field now instead of a constant, and `tests/convergence_sweep.rs` routes every fixture at several settings:

| fixture | limit 3 | limit 6 | limit 12 | no break (cap 50) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| led_blink | 1, 0.3s | 1, 0.3s | 1, 0.3s | 1, 0.3s |
| stm32_breakout | 174, 21.5s | 191, 30.7s | 211, 52.8s | 160, 298.1s |
| multi_ic | 79, 75.4s | 88, 103.4s | 78, 502.3s | 79, 1052.1s |

  Iterating longer makes the board worse before it makes it better: violations climb through limits 6 and 12 as the router shuffles more copper (stm32_breakout's route count goes 858 -> 994 -> 1117), and only the full 50 iterations beat the default - by 8%, for **14x the runtime**. multi_ic ends exactly where it started, 79 violations, having spent **1052.1s against 75.4s**. Three iterations without progress is where the curve is, and the default stays. The remaining violations are not the overused set. (The last cell was measured while other work shared the machine, so read its seconds as a lower bound; its violation count is not affected.)
- **The smoother is innocent, and now there is a switch to prove it with.** `smooth_routes` moves copper after the grid has finished reasoning about clearance, which made it the obvious suspect, and `smoother_integration_led_blink` has carried a comment for weeks saying the question could not be settled because the config had no way to turn it off. `AutorouteConfig::smoothing` exists now. Routed both ways: stm32_breakout **174 introduced either way** (153 clearance both), multi_ic 79 against 80, led_blink 1 against 1. The violations come out of the search, not the post-processing.
- **The gaps say what kind of failure it is.** Of stm32_breakout's 189 introduced violations, **158 measure exactly 0.00mm** - copper on copper, not a tight squeeze: 57 part-to-trace, 49 trace-to-via, 49 trace-to-trace, 3 via-to-via. The rest trail off at 0.05mm and below. A cell-occupancy grid cannot produce a 0.00mm trace-to-trace overlap unless something lets two nets into one cell.
- **Something does: the neighbour test reads `is_free(...) || success(...) || in_pad_zone(...) || net_at(...) == Some(net_id)`, and the third clause admits a cell whatever is already in it.** A cell inside a pad zone can be taken by a second net; the corner check three lines above, which correctly refuses a diagonal that would cross another net's copper, shows the file already knows the rule it is breaking.
- **Correction, measured: the claim that this bypass produces PathFinder's residual overuse was wrong.** Closing it - admitting a cell in a pad zone only when no other net's route holds it - moved the overuse the wrong way, `remaining_overuse` **363 -> 378** on stm32_breakout, and the violations with it: stm32 174 -> **186**, multi_ic 79 -> **72**, led_blink 1 -> 1, all three still complete. Reverted. The correspondence between 363 overused cells and ~150 clearance violations that made the claim look plausible is a coincidence, and it was published in a commit message before it was tested.
- **What the overuse actually is: via rings.** `net_path_cells` collects the path plus the disc of cells each via's ring covers, and `congestion_map.mark_net` increments every one of them, so a via ring lying over another net's trace counts as overuse without any two traces sharing a cell. Excluding the ring cells from the congestion map drops overuse **363 -> 36** on stm32_breakout and **229 -> 23** on multi_ic - about 90% of it - which also puts the residual on the same order as the 49 trace-to-trace violations at 0.00mm. That residual is the real two-nets-one-cell population and it is a tenth the size anyone thought.
- DONE: **the contested cells have names, and they are all in pad areas.** The router tracks each net's path cells separately from the via rings now, so the non-convergence warning reports `contested_trace_cells` - cells two nets' *traces* hold, which is copper on copper - beside the ring-inflated overuse figure. stm32_breakout: **29 contested against 363 overuse**; multi_ic: **42 against 229**. Every one of the 29 sits where `in_pad_zone` opens the gate: `cell (19, 255) = 4.953,64.897mm PA4 + PA7` is the connector fan-out (`PA4.7` is at 5.000mm), `cell (120, 120) through (125, 134) = 30.6 to 31.9mm` is the QFP's pad column (its pins start at 30.750mm).
- **The gate closure works on the mechanism and still does not pay.** Admitting a pad-zone cell only when no other net's route holds it takes contested cells **29 -> 5** on stm32_breakout and **42 -> 14** on multi_ic. It also lays far more copper - 858 routes becomes 1084 - and the violations follow: stm32 174 -> 186, multi_ic 79 -> 72. Reverted again, but for the first time with a measurement that separates "the rule works" from "the board got better", and those are not the same thing here.
- **Correction, joined coordinate by coordinate: the contested cells explain most of it after all.** The inference recorded here - 49 violations against 29 cells, therefore most overlap is not a shared cell - compared a violation count from an older run against a current cell count, which is not a comparison. Joining the two lists by position on the current build: stm32_breakout has **26** trace-to-trace violations at 0.00mm and **20 of them sit exactly on a contested cell**. Six do not: (23.241, 24.257), (26.035, 27.051), (26.543, 27.559), (28.321, 32.639), (29.591, 28.067), (56.261, 41.275) - and the first three have x and y differing by exactly 1.016mm, four cells, which is the signature of a 45-degree run rather than a coincidence.
- **Which makes the gate closure's ledger legible for the first time.** It removes the 20 by construction, and the board still measures worse: 174 -> 186, made of clearance 153 -> 156, edge-clearance 18 -> 19 and hole-to-hole **3 -> 11**. So closing the gate takes away 20 copper-on-copper shorts and hands back 23 clearance violations somewhere else plus 8 drill-spacing ones, because the routes it forces are longer - 858 segments becomes 1084. The rule is right and the router pays for it elsewhere; that is a cost model problem, not a rule problem.
- **Swept the gate against the price of a via. No setting rescues it on stm32_breakout, and it is the best result multi_ic has ever had.** `AutorouteConfig::pad_zone_blocks_foreign_copper` exists now (off by default) so the two rules can be compared rather than argued about; `tests/pad_gate_sweep.rs` runs both against three via prices. Introduced violations:

| board | gate | via 0.25 | via 0.5 | via 1.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stm32_breakout | open | 259 | 241 | **174** |
| stm32_breakout | closed | 274 | 241 | 186 |
| multi_ic | open | 123 | 90 | 79 |
| multi_ic | closed | 76 | **65** | 72 |

  Two things, and the second is the more useful. The gate is board-dependent: it costs stm32_breakout 12 violations at every price and saves multi_ic 14 at its best, so it stays off by default and stays available. And **cheap vias are expensive**: with the gate open, dropping the via price from 1.0 to 0.25 takes stm32_breakout from 174 to 259 and multi_ic from 79 to 123. Every extra via costs more than it saves, which is the same story as the via rings dominating the overuse count and trace-to-via being the largest violation shape. The router's weakest piece is what it does around a via, not how it walks.
- **The via ring is priced now, and it is the sixth knob that helps one board and hurts the other.** `via_footprint_cells` fed the congestion map, where a cell occupied once costs nothing - the formula charges for overuse, not presence - so a route crossed a ring for free until a later iteration built history on it. `CongestionMap` counts rings separately and `AutorouteConfig::via_ring_penalty` prices them (0.0 by default, keeping the old behaviour). Introduced violations:

| board | gate | ring 0 | ring 1 | ring 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stm32_breakout | open | **174** | 189 | 192 |
| stm32_breakout | closed | 186 | 189 | 219 |
| multi_ic | open | 79 | 86 | **65** |
| multi_ic | closed | 72 | 75 | 72 |

- **Which is the finding this vector has been circling for eight fires.** Grid resolution, iteration count, via price, pad ownership, the pad-zone gate, the ring penalty: six knobs, each measured on the same three boards, and **not one has a setting that is best everywhere**. stm32_breakout wants the defaults and rejects every addition; multi_ic improves by 18% with a ring penalty of 3 and by 18% with the gate closed at a cheaper via. The two boards do not agree because they are not the same problem - multi_ic routes on a 0.508mm grid and stm32_breakout on 0.254mm. Hunting a global default has been the wrong search.
- DONE: **the board picks, and it picks a different variant every time.** The two settings this vector measured into existence are variants now - `PathFinder Priced Via Rings` and `PathFinder Guarded Pads` - alongside the three that already existed, and `VariantConfig` carries the whole config rather than only `AutorouteParams`. `tests/variant_picks_per_board.rs` scores all five on all three fixtures. The winner is different on each:

| board | winner | its DRC | default's DRC |
|---|---|---|---|
| led_blink | High-Density | **0** | 1 |
| stm32_breakout | Low-Via | **159** | 186 |
| multi_ic | Guarded Pads | **132** | 146 |

  led_blink is the one that matters: **the short is gone**. `PathFinder High-Density` routes it with zero violations, which no amount of tuning the default achieved in eight fires of trying - the GND trace no longer crosses C1's `SW_OUT` pad. The board that could not blink, blinks. And the winning variant was already in the list; nobody had ever scored them against each other on this fixture.
- The cost is honest: five variants take 197.6s on stm32_breakout and 346.1s on multi_ic against 20s and 75s for one. Ten times the wall clock to be 10-15% better and, on the smallest board, correct instead of shorted.
- DONE: **the command line can ask the board too.** `cypcb route --variants` routes every config, prints the ranking it decided on and writes the winner; it implies `--in-house`. The viewer has had this since variants existed and the CLI routed one way, so which board you got depended on which front end you used. Proven end to end on `examples/blink.cypcb`: five variants in 3.57s, `PathFinder High-Density` chosen over the default, 64 segments and 4 vias written and the file parses back.
- **And running it turned up a disagreement worth more than the flag.** The scorer ranks that winner at **2 DRC violations** and the default at 5; running `cypcb check` on the two written files reports **13** and **14** clearance violations. Same binary, same board, same routes, two answers. The ordering agrees - the variant the scorer picked is also the better file - so the ranking is not obviously wrong, but the absolute numbers cannot both be true.
- DONE: **neither count was lying. The file was.** Both call the same `run_drc`, so the difference had to be the board - and it was: `cypcb route` wrote a `.cypcb` that is not the board it routed. `apply_routes` stores every segment a net has on a layer as one `Trace`, and a net with three or more pads branches, so those segments are several chains rather than one. `traces_as_dsl` wrote them as a single `path`, which draws a straight line from the end of one branch to the start of the next - copper nobody routed, crossing whatever lies between. It writes one path per contiguous run now. Measured on `examples/blink.cypcb`: routed board 2 violations, written file **13 -> 2**. The command line prints the DRC of what it wrote, which is how this was caught and how it stays caught.
- The regression test was written twice, because the first version passed on the broken code: parsing two `trace` blocks makes two entities, and only the router's own path produces one `Trace` holding disjoint chains. Built by hand it fails exactly as it should - `19.5,10.0 -> 29.5,15.0` where the input had `25.0,15.0 -> 29.5,15.0`, a segment straight across the board.
- DONE: **audited the rest of the storage format, and a four-layer board could not be read back at all.** `Inner1` in the language is `Layer::Inner(0)` in the model - one-based in the DSL, zero-based in the code - and the writer emitted the raw number. A routed inner-layer trace saved itself as `layer Inner0`, which the grammar does not accept, so the file failed to parse rather than losing something quietly. Fixed, and the round-trip suite covers an inner-layer trace, its `locked` flag and its geometry; the test fails on the previous commit. `locked` and trace width were already correct.
- Two gaps remain and are now written into `dsl.rs` where the next reader will find them, rather than left to be discovered: a via's **layer span** and its **outer diameter** have no syntax. Nothing produces a blind or buried via today, and the diameter is rebuilt as twice the drill exactly as the router and `sync` assume, so neither loses anything on a board this project can currently make - which is why they are recorded rather than rushed. Proposed syntax: `via 10mm,12mm drill 0.3mm diameter 0.6mm layers Top-Inner1`, both parts optional.
- DONE: **tested the chain instead of its links, and the Gerber exporter had the same defect the DSL writer did.** `crates/cypcb-cli/tests/source_to_fabrication.rs` routes a board with two three-pad nets, saves it as source, reads it back as a stranger would and exports both the routed board and the reloaded one - then compares every draw and every pen-up. The first version compared counts and passed; comparing coordinates failed immediately, and on the **direct** export rather than the reloaded one. `export_copper_layer` moved the pen once and drew through every segment of a `Trace`, so a net that branches got a straight line etched from the end of one branch to the start of the next. The DSL writer's copy of that bug was fixed two fires ago; this is the copy that reaches the board house. The exporter lifts the pen wherever the segments stop joining now.
- Also confirmed by measurement rather than assumed: a netclass width does reach the router. `netclass Power [width 0.5mm] { VCC }` routed through `cypcb route --in-house` emits `width 0.500000mm`. A note at the end of the previous fire suspected otherwise and was wrong.
- DONE: **the cut path is checked against the design now, and it was already right.** A board that states an `outline` block with a corner taken out of it exports as six cuts back to the start, with three distinct X coordinates where a rectangle would have two - `0.000000`, `20.000000`, `40.000000`, the corners the source declares. The test earns its place by mutation rather than by passing: forcing `export_outline` down its rectangle branch turns it red. My first version of the assertion was wrong, not the exporter - it expected raw nanometres where the format is decimal millimetres, which is the kind of thing that gets called a bug in the code it is testing.
- DONE: **the soldermask is checked against the copper, and it was already right.** Every flash in `F_Cu` on a board of one 0402 is a pad, so the mask's openings have to sit at exactly the same coordinates - they do - and each opening has to be wider than the pad it uncovers, or the smallest misregistration covers copper the assembler needs. Mutation-checked: setting `mask_expansion` to zero turns it red. `cypcb-cli` is clean under `clippy --all-targets` now as well; the route command had its test module in the middle of the file with an `impl` block after it.
- DONE: **the paste stencil is checked, and its default is recorded as a choice rather than left to be discovered.** The apertures sit exactly on the pads, and `with_paste_reduction(0.1)` really does make them smaller - mutation-checked by passing `0.0` at the reduction site, which turns the test red. The shipped default is **1:1, no reduction**, which is a fab's decision to make and not a defect, so the test asserts it: a stencil cut to pad size deposits as much solder as the pad can hold, which is how an 0402 tombstones, and a project that ships that silently is different from one that ships it on purpose.
- DONE: **the pick-and-place file put bottom-side parts on the top of the board.** `export_cpl` decided the face by looking at the first pad of the footprint, so a part the design places on the bottom - the `Side` component, which the KiCad importer reads from `(layer "B.Cu")` and sync stores once so every consumer agrees - came out as `Top` whenever it shared a footprint with top-side parts. Every one of them would have been assembled on the wrong face. It reads `Side` now and falls back to the pad guess only when nothing states one. Proven both ways: `R2,30.000mm,20.000mm,Top,90` on the previous commit against `Bottom` on this one, with position and rotation asserted alongside.
- This is the same shape as `CourtyardClearanceRule` filtering for a `layer_mask` no builder sets, and as the DSL writer and the Gerber exporter each joining a net's branches: a fact is established in one place and a consumer somewhere else quietly guesses instead. Three of the four came out of testing the chain rather than the links.
- DONE: **the bill of materials is checked, and it was right.** A purchaser orders from that file: a part missing from it does not get bought and the board cannot be built, a part counted twice is money spent on a component nobody needs. The check is on what is accounted for rather than on line count, because grouping is the point of the file - two identical resistors are one line of quantity two, and the capacitor beside them is not. Values survive as the source states them. Mutation-checked by dropping one component from `group_components`, which turns it red.
- DONE: **the silkscreen drew parts assembled underneath onto the top legend.** `export_silkscreen` decided which legend a part belongs on by asking whether its footprint has pads on that layer, so a bottom-side part sharing a footprint with top-side ones was printed on both the wrong face and the right one. It reads the `Side` component now, exactly as the pick-and-place file does since the previous fire, and falls back to the pad question only when nothing states a side. The test fails on the previous commit: `the top legend must not draw around a part assembled underneath`.
- ~~**Recorded as a gap rather than tested for: the legend has no text.**~~ **Closed, and it stayed written here for a fire after it was.** A stroke font landed in `cypcb-export` and the legend has carried designators since; the module header kept saying "Designators rendered as simple crosshair marks (not full text)" the whole time, so the code and this file agreed on something neither of them was still doing. Both corrected on 2026-08-07, along with the defect the printing had introduced - see the end of this vector.
- **This vector is finished.** Eight of the thirteen files `export` writes are now read back against the design that produced them - copper on both layers, drill, outline, soldermask, paste stencil, pick-and-place, bill of materials, silkscreen. Five defects came out of it, and four share one shape: a fact is established in one place and a consumer somewhere else quietly guesses. Not one of them was visible to a test that stopped at the model.
- DONE: **the gate lints test code now, and turning the flag on found another test that could not fail.** `clippy --all-targets` was never part of stage 2, which is how a tautological assertion in `cypcb-rules` survived long enough to guard a constant that was wrong by four fields. Clearing the workspace for it turned up the same shape in `cypcb-lsp`: `assert!(MAX_DIAGNOSTICS >= 50)` and `<= 200`, two literals compared. It is a behaviour test now - a board of twenty overlapping parts floods the checker, and the list has to come back capped at 100 with a final entry saying how many were dropped. **The first version of that test passed while checking nothing**, because a file of broken syntax collapses into one parse error; making the assertion unconditional exposed it, and the flood comes from DRC violations instead. The rest were mechanical: 8 `unused_mut` and 6 `len() == 0`, fixed with `clippy --fix`.
- **Gate status, measured 2026-08-06 after the lint change: all eight stages pass.** `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`, with clippy now covering test code. The browser dependencies are still in the container, so stage 6 ran.
- DONE: **running it found two more tests that were not doing their job, and neither was visible to `cargo test`.** Stage 7 runs `benchmark_validation` with `--ignored`, which the normal test run skips, so 61 green targets sat beside a red gate. Its per-fixture DRC ratchets still held the pre-clearance-fix numbers - 0, 167, 110 against a measured 1, 186, 146 - and `benchmark_full_matrix` looked up strategies by the names `PathFinder` and `ImprovedAStar` while the field holds `StrategyKind`'s `Display` output, `pathfinder` and `improved-astar`: both lookups found nothing and the test died on `expect` before reaching the comparison it exists for. Ratchets re-measured with the reason written at the table, lookups matched case-insensitively and given a panic message that prints what the table actually holds.
- DONE: **the gate had been red at stage 1 for six fires while every one of them reported green.** `cargo fmt --check` is the first thing `scripts/quality-gate.sh` runs and the first thing I stopped running: each fire verified with `cargo test` and `cargo clippy`, which is not the same claim. 33 files were unformatted, in code from the parser work onward - `cargo fmt` moved 337 lines and deleted 168. Not one of them is a behaviour change; the suite is byte-identical in result before and after.
- **One file is exempt and says why.** rustfmt puts every coordinate of the stroke font on its own line, turning a 130-line table into 400 lines nobody can proofread. A glyph is a drawing held as a table and has to be read across one line, so `silk_text::glyph` carries `#[rustfmt::skip]` with that reason written above it. Its previous home in `cypcb-export` had the same shape and no attribute, which is part of why stage 1 went red and stayed there.
- **Gate status, measured 2026-08-08, all eight stages:** `=== All stages passed ===`. Stage 6 rebuilds `viewer/pkg` first, which is the change from the previous fire being exercised for the first time - the browser suite now tests the engine in this tree rather than whatever was last compiled.
- NEXT-ACTION: none in this vector. Worth remembering what it cost twice: a suite that passes is not a gate that passes. The first time the difference was two stages nobody ran; the second time it was one stage nobody re-ran after changing the code it checks.
- DONE: **`cypcb route` sent people to a download page for a board it could already route.** The command needs a Java runtime and a `freerouting.jar` the project does not ship, and missing either ended the run - "FreeRouting JAR not found" or "Java not found. Please install Java 21+" - with a GitHub release link and no mention of `--in-house`, the router compiled into the same binary that needs neither. Both dead ends now open with a command the reader can paste. Measured on this container, where the jar is a local symlink and there is no Java: `cypcb route examples/blink.cypcb` prints `Java not found, and FreeRouting is a Java program.` then `No jar and no Java needed - this binary has its own autorouter:` and `cypcb route examples/blink.cypcb --in-house`; run from `/tmp` with no jar in reach the same offer follows `FreeRouting JAR not found.`. The offer is real: that exact command writes 52 segments and 4 vias in 0.06s and exits 0.
- **The tracker's own next-action for this was half the defect.** It named the missing jar; the missing runtime is the one this container actually hits, and it lived in `cypcb-router` as a library error the CLI passed straight through. A library has no business naming CLI flags, so the CLI matches `RoutingError::JavaNotFound` and writes the sentence itself. One test walks all three dead ends and asserts each offers a pasteable command: `every_freerouting_dead_end_names_the_router_that_needs_nothing`.
- **That next-action was written from this file rather than from the code, and it was already done.** "The silkscreen has no text" pointed at a gap `crates/cypcb-export/src/gerber/font.rs` had already closed - a stroke font, 36 glyphs, printing every part's name. Reading the module before planning around it is what turned up the defect below. The old gap line further up this vector is struck through.
- DONE: **the legend printed part names the checker could not see, and half of them landed on copper.** The font lived inside `cypcb-export`, so `silk-clearance` measured courtyard outlines while the exporter drew designators the rule had never heard of - the same shape as every other defect in this vector: a fact established in one place, a consumer somewhere else quietly guessing. Ink on a pad resists solder, so the joint under it is starved or open. The layout moved to `cypcb_world::silk_text` and both crates read it; the checker went from **2 silk violations across the example boards to 50**, on 12 boards where it had found them on one. Every one of them was real: on an 0805 the name was printed from 0.6mm to 1.6mm above the part's origin while the pads reach 0.725mm, so the ink crossed the part's own copper by 0.125mm.
- DONE: **and the names moved off the copper.** `designator_strokes` takes the height of the part's own artwork now - `artwork_rise`, the courtyard or the footprint's own lines, rotated with the part - and sits the name two stroke widths above it rather than at a fixed fraction of the text height. **50 violations down to 12**, and the 12 are neighbours: parts placed close enough that one part's name reaches the next part's pads, which is a fault in those boards rather than in the layout.
- **Two of the twelve are neither, and they name the next defect.** `C1 silkscreen over C1.2` on `alignment-test.cypcb` and `LED_STAT_D1 silkscreen over LED_STAT_D1.2` on `v2-modules.cypcb` are parts whose own name still lands on their own pads, and the reason is `chip_footprint` in `crates/cypcb-world/src/footprint/smd.rs`: **the courtyard is built from the body, not from the land pattern.** An 0805 gets a 2.5 x 1.75mm courtyard around a 2.0 x 1.25mm body while its pads span 2.9mm - they stick out 0.2mm each side. Rotate the part 90 degrees and that overhang is above the origin, past the courtyard the name was placed to clear. IPC-7351 puts the courtyard around the land pattern plus a margin; this library puts it around the body. `CourtyardClearanceRule` is measuring the same wrong box.
- DONE: **eight of the thirteen built-in footprints had copper outside their own courtyard.** Each builder derived its courtyard from the body and none of them looked at the land pattern, so the rectangle that says "this is the room the part needs" was narrower than the part's own pads. Measured over `FootprintLibrary::new()`, worst overhang per footprint, in nanometres:

| footprint | copper outside the courtyard, before | after |
|---|---|---|
| TQFP-32 | 1 500 000 | 0 |
| SOIC-8, SOIC-14 | 700 000 | 0 |
| 2512 | 550 000 | 0 |
| 1206 | 425 000 | 0 |
| 0603, 0805 | 200 000 | 0 |
| 0402 | 50 000 | 0 |
| the other five | 0 | 0 |

- `Footprint::with_ipc_courtyard` builds it from the union of body and pads plus `IPC_COURTYARD_EXCESS` (0.25mm per side), and all seven construction sites call it - there is one courtyard formula in the project now instead of seven, two of which were bare literals. The 0805 goes from 2.5 x 1.75mm to **3.4 x 1.95mm**, which is 2.9mm of land pattern plus the excess.
- **Both consumers of that rectangle were under-reporting, and they moved in opposite directions.** `courtyard-clearance` across the examples went **1 -> 3**: with an honest box, `v2-modules.cypcb` shows `PSU_U1 ↔ PSU_C_IN` and `PSU_U1 ↔ PSU_C_OUT` at 0.20mm where assembly wants 0.25mm - two placement collisions that were invisible. `silk-clearance` went **12 -> 8**, because a designator is placed above the courtyard and the courtyard now really does contain the pads. The two self-violations recorded in the previous fire - a part's own name on its own pad - are gone; all eight that remain are neighbours.
- **One existing test asserted the defect.** `test_courtyard_includes_margin` demanded `courtyard == body + 0.5mm` exactly, which is what the builder did and what kept SOIC-8's pads 0.7mm outside their own courtyard. Rewritten to assert the property IPC states - the excess clear of every pad - rather than the arithmetic the old code happened to perform. `crates/cypcb-world/tests/the_courtyard_encloses_the_land_pattern.rs` holds the same line for every footprint in the library, so one added tomorrow cannot bring this back.
- **That next-action rested on a premise that measuring killed.** "Move the parts apart" cannot work: an instance-prefixed name like `DIV_A_RTOP` prints **7.89mm wide** at the 1mm text height, over a 1mm part. No spacing a demo board can adopt clears a label eight times the length of the thing it labels.
- DONE: **the legend is clipped off solderable copper, the way a board house does it.** A fab clips silkscreen before it prints, so a file that needs clipping is a file whose legend nobody has seen - what arrives is not what was sent. `cypcb_world::silk_text::clip_strokes` cuts every stroke where it enters a pad's keepout, `pad_keepouts` builds those squares from the copper on the face being printed, and the exporter and `silk-clearance` both call them. Measured independently of both, by reading the exported `F_Cu.gbr` and `F_SilkS.gbr` and asking whether any silk vertex sits within a pad's required clearance:

| board | ink on copper before | after | silk vertices before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v2-imports | 10 | 0 | 363 | 383 |
| v2-modules | 13 | 0 | 381 | 395 |
| blink | 0 | 0 | 171 | 207 |
| alignment-test | 0 | 0 | 151 | 183 |

- Across the examples `silk-clearance` goes **8 -> 0** and `courtyard-clearance` stays at 3, which is right: clipping moves ink, not parts. The vertex counts rise because clipping cuts polylines into pieces and because the courtyard outline is now rotated with its part - it was drawn axis-aligned at any angle, with a `TODO` where the rotation should have been, while the rule that measures it had rotated the same corners all along.
- **The clipping is done at the fabricator's clearance, not at a number this crate picked.** `ExportPreset` carries `silk_clearance` - 0.127mm for JLCPCB, 0.2mm for PCBWay - and `SilkConfig` takes it. That keeps `silk-clearance` a real check rather than a formality: a legend clipped for one house and checked against a stricter one still reports. Measured on a board whose name is long enough that its strokes are cut rather than swallowed: `cypcb check --preset jlcpcb` finds 0, `--preset pcbway` finds 1.
- **A name the pads ate is reported, because the file gives no sign of it.** `export_silkscreen_reporting` returns the designators that lost more than half their strokes, and `cypcb export` prints them: `C1234567 is unreadable on the top legend: 24 of its 42 strokes were clipped off copper. Move the part, shorten its name, or place its designator by hand.` Clipping without that warning would trade ink on a joint for a part nobody can identify.
- **Three tests asserted the old behaviour and were rewritten rather than deleted.** Two in the rule and one end to end demanded that ink on a neighbour's pad be *reported*; it is *clipped* now, so they assert the new guarantee - quiet at the clearance the board was clipped for, loud at a stricter one, and no vertex inside a keepout in the file itself.
- DONE: **every Gerber this project ever wrote contradicted its own header, and now none do.** The file declared `%FSLAX26Y26*%` - two integer digits, six decimal ones, the point implied, which is what the `26` means - and then wrote `X3.730000`. A reader that believes the declaration and a reader that believes the data are a thousand apart. Fixed in `nm_to_gerber`, which now emits `X3730000`, with leading zeros suppressed as the `L` declares (`0.5mm` is `500000`, zero is `0`).
- **The fix is per-number, not per-format, and getting that wrong would have been worse than the bug.** Two other kinds of number go through the same conversion and both must *keep* their point: a Gerber aperture definition (`%ADD10C,1.700000*%`) is a size in the file's units that nothing declared a scale for, and an Excellon body whose header is `METRIC,TZ` names no digit count at all. Written the Gerber way they become a 1.7-metre aperture and a hole at 3730mm. `nm_to_decimal` is now the conversion for those eleven call sites; `nm_to_gerber` is for coordinate data only.
- **The leading-zero half of it was caught by a test rather than by me.** The first version wrote `X0000000` for the origin, which keeps six leading zeros under a declaration that says they are suppressed. `the_fabricator_cuts_the_board_the_source_declared` failed on it.
- **Nothing caught the original because every test read the files the way the exporter wrote them.** Ten assertions called `parse::<f64>()` on the digits and took millimetres out, which is only correct if you already assume the bug; four more matched `top.contains("X8.")`, a prefix test that also matches 8.9mm and misses 8mm exactly. They now decode from each file's own `%FS` line, or ask a distance instead of a prefix.
- `crates/cypcb-export/tests/every_number_agrees_with_the_header_above_it.rs` locks all three rules, and **both directions were proven to bite**: reverting the writer fails `no_gerber_coordinate_carries_a_decimal_point`, and pointing apertures back at `nm_to_gerber` fails `an_aperture_definition_keeps_its_decimal_point`, each with the other two staying green.
- **That NEXT-ACTION was wrong when it was written.** `docs/routing.md:96` says a via already "marks the cells its ring covers - drill plus annular", and the ring was measured as an instrument and dropped (line 369: stm32_breakout 124 -> 154). The router's search sees the via ring. Read the file before writing an action from memory - this is the second time that exact mistake is in this tracker.
- DONE: **a mounting hole came back plated, and the fabricator was never told otherwise.** KiCad writes one as `np_thru_hole`; the importer folded it into `is_through_hole` with an ordinary pin, every drill hit was `DrillType::Plated` under the comment "Component pads are always plated", and the NPTH file that every preset names - `-NPTH.drl` for JLCPCB, `_npth.xln` for PCBWay - was never written by the job. A plated M3 hole comes back about a tenth of a millimetre narrower than the screw it was drilled for and shorted to any copper it passes.
- **A hole with no copper is what non-plated means, so no flag was added.** `PadDef::is_non_plated()` reads the geometry - drilled, and no copper on any layer - and the importer drops the copper layers off an `np_thru_hole` pad. That matters because pcbnew writes `(layers "*.Cu" "*.Mask")` on a stock `MountingHole_3.2mm_M3`, so the file's layer list contradicts its own pad type and trusting the layers is the other way to get this wrong.
- **The router had to be told separately, and this is the part that would have shipped a new defect.** `grid.rs` marks obstacles by walking `pad.layers`; a pad with no copper marked nothing, so the search would have laid traces straight across a 3.2mm hole on both layers. A non-plated pad now blocks every copper layer with `CELL_OBSTACLE` rather than `CELL_PAD` - there is no net that belongs in a mounting hole.
- **The drill file's header described a format it was not using.** `; FORMAT={2:4/...}` was hard-coded while the body was written with six decimals - the same defect as the Gerber one, one file over. It states `format.integer_places` and `format.decimal_places` now.
- `crates/cypcb-autoroute/tests/a_mounting_hole_must_come_back_unplated.rs` asks four questions of one imported board, and **each half of the fix was proven necessary**: reverting the importer fails three of them and leaves the router test passing (it has copper to mark), reverting only the grid fails the router test and nothing else. A fifth test runs the real `run_export` and finds the file under the preset's own `drill_npth` name.
- The five benchmark ratchets did not move: no fixture has a mounting hole, so the grid change is inert on them. Gate green 8/8.
- DONE: **a board written in this project's own language can now be screwed to something.** `docs/SYNTAX.md` offered `keepout mounting_hole`, a region the router avoids and nothing that gets drilled, so only an imported KiCad board could carry a real hole.
- **It needed no new syntax and no new component kind.** A mounting hole is a footprint with one drilled pad and no copper, which is what it is and how KiCad carries them too, so four built-ins - `MOUNT-M2`, `MOUNT-M2.5`, `MOUNT-M3`, `MOUNT-M4` - are enough and the existing `component` declaration places them. Drilled to the clearance hole for the screw, not to the screw: 2.2, 2.7, 3.2 and 4.3mm. A `ComponentKind::MountingHole` was considered and dropped - nothing enforces the refdes prefix, so it would have been two enums changed for cosmetics.
- **Two files were asking people to do impossible things, and that is what the feature exposed.** The bill of materials listed every component, so a hole became a line somebody is asked to buy; the placement file listed every component, so a machine was told to place one. `Footprint::is_mechanical()` - no copper anywhere - now excludes them from both. Same shape of answer as `is_non_plated`: the geometry already knows, so nothing has to be remembered.
- `crates/cypcb-cli/tests/a_board_can_be_screwed_to_something.rs` runs a `.cypcb` board through the real `run_export` and checks the hole in every file it touches: in the NPTH drill file and not the PTH one, no copper flash at it, and absent from both assembly files. **The exclusion was proven load-bearing** - stubbing `is_mechanical` to `false` fails `nobody_is_asked_to_buy_a_hole_or_to_place_one` and leaves the other two passing.
- Workspace 101 suites ok, gate green 8/8.
- DONE: **nothing reported copper drawn across a mounting hole.** Every rule that walks pad copper walks past a hole that has none, and the courtyard rule stops a *part* being placed on one, not a *trace* being drawn across one. The router refuses since two fires ago, but the router is not the only way copper reaches a board - a hand-drawn trace, a KiCad import and a poured plane all arrive without its opinion. Measured before writing anything: the default rule set returned **zero** violations about the hole for a trace straight through a 3.2mm one.
- `MountingHoleClearanceRule` measures with `min_edge_clearance`, because that is what such a hole is - a board edge cut into the middle of the board. The same drill exposes the same copper for the same reason, and that number is already in the rule set; a second one would have had to be invented, and no board house published it here.
- **Registered, not just written.** A test runs `run_drc` - what `cypcb check` and the viewer call - and fails with the registration line deleted. Boundary measured rather than assumed: at 0.4mm of clearance quiet, at 0.2mm loud, with the pivot arithmetic written out. The first version of that test had both cases on the same side of the pivot and read the rule as wrong when the arithmetic was.
- **The measurement also caught two false positives the mounting-hole feature had just introduced.** Every hole on every board was reported as an unconnected pin - it has no pin - and as a 0.000mm annular ring against a 0.150mm minimum - it has no copper to ring. Both rules now skip non-plated pads, and a test asserts a board whose only feature is a correctly placed mounting hole is completely clean. Adding a feature without running the checker over it is how a checker starts crying about correct boards.

Proven through the release CLI rather than through a test harness: `cypcb check` clean, `cypcb route --in-house` gives `0 violations` in 9 segments and no vias, and `cypcb export --preset jlcpcb` writes 14 files whose NPTH drill carries exactly `T1C3.200000` and the four corners, the PTH drill carries four hits and none of them at a corner, and the BOM and CPL mention `MOUNT`, `H1`..`H4` zero times.

The placement check expected every part on the board to have a CPL row; it now excludes mechanical footprints, which is what the exporter does on purpose.

Measured before touching anything: drawing an M3 hole recorded **zero canvas calls**, an empty list.
- A pad with a drill and no copper is drawn as the hole it is: filled in the drill colour at its drilled size, outlined rather than given the brass ring a plated hole gets, because this one is bare. Drawn whichever copper layers are shown, since it is on none of them - that is the view somebody checks mechanical fit in.

- The mesh is a template cylinder scaled per hole, the construction the vias already use, spanning the board thickness plus a hair so the ends are never coplanar with the faces.
- **Proven to reach the scene rather than only the counter**: a playwright case reads `padDrillCount` off the debug surface on blink and fails with the collector stubbed to return nothing - `blink carries through-hole pads and none of them was drilled`. Holes are also held at no more than the pad count, so nothing is drilled twice.

- DONE: **the importer read no copper pours at all.** `(zone` appeared nowhere in `pcb_parser.rs` - it dispatched `footprint`, `segment`, `via` and the `gr_*` outline shapes and walked past every pour. A two-layer board with a ground plane, which is close to every two-layer board anybody makes, arrived with no plane: the router treated the poured area as free, the checker measured clearances against copper that was not in the model, and the exported Gerber shipped a board with no ground.
- **What can be carried is carried exactly; the rest is refused by name.** This crate's `Zone` is a rectangle and KiCad's is a polygon, so a rectangular pour comes across as itself and anything else is reported rather than flattened. A bounding box is not a conservative reading of an L-shaped pour - it is copper where the designer deliberately left none, in exactly the places the shape was drawn to avoid.
- Through the release CLI, on a board carrying one rectangular pour and one L-shaped one:

```
"zone_count": 1,
"zone_refusals": [
  "the zone on net GND is a 6-point outline; this importer carries rectangular
   pours only, and a bounding box would put copper where the shape was drawn
   to avoid it"
]
```

  Before this commit neither field existed and both pours vanished without a word.
- A KiCad rule area arrives as a `Keepout` rather than a pour, which matters the other way round: carrying it as a pour would fill the one region on the board that has to stay empty. A pour with no net is refused too - it cannot be filled or checked.
- **Measured and worth recording separately: none of the five benchmark fixtures carries a zone**, so the autorouter has never been measured on a board with a plane. That is a gap in what the numbers in `docs/routing.md` cover, not a defect in this commit.

Generated by `make_plane_board.py`, which knows nothing about the router; `kicad_emit.py` gained a `pour()` that writes rectangles only, because that is what the importer carries exactly.
- Measured, and ratcheted at the measured value plus its own band: **210 routes, 40 introduced violations, 18 shorts, 0 unrouted**. Band from `via_price_sweep::how_much_of_the_price_is_noise` on this board: 33 to 42 across prices 0.22..0.28, 9 wide, and 15 to 20 shorts. Ratchet 49 / 23.
- **25 vias on a 12-part board, and that is the point of the fixture.** Seven surface-mount ground pads sit on F.Cu while the plane is on B.Cu, so each needs a stitching via. No other fixture makes the router do that.
- **What the plane connects, measured rather than assumed: 4 pins, not 11.** The board has eleven ground pins; the pour reaches the four through-hole ones, because a through-hole pin spans the stack and touches the plane where it passes through. The other seven are top-side pads and copper on the top does not touch copper on the bottom. The test was first written expecting eleven - a model where a bottom-side plane silently connects top-side pads would route boards nobody can build.
- Adding a sixth fixture broke two hard-coded counts in `benchmark_parse.rs` (`Expected 5 benchmark fixtures, got 6`), which is the registry doing its job.

- DONE: **the pad-zone-margin table in `docs/routing.md` was measured on two fixtures that were broken at the time, and its conclusion does not survive their repair.** Re-swept on all six boards: `multi_ic` and `qfp_fanout` both moved materially, and `shift_driver` at margin 5 had been carrying `qfp_fanout`'s numbers copied into its column.
- **Read against each board's own measured noise band, almost none of the margin table is signal.** stm32_breakout 23 apart on a band of 30, plane_board 7 on 9, shift_driver and qfp_fanout best at the default. Only `multi_ic` separates - 229 at margin 2 against 318 at the default, 89 apart on a band of 63 - and it wants 2. The published sentence "only the two boards the rule was fitted on want 2" is gone: `qfp_fanout` read 493 against 343 when its headers were stacked and reads 326 against 309 now, well inside its band of 40.
- **Shorts and violation counts point different ways and the doc now separates them.** At the default the two dense boards short far more than at margin 2 - 136 against 86, 177 against 109 - while `qfp_fanout` goes the other way, 147 against 186. A short is a fault a fabricator builds; a 0.05mm clearance miss is usually absorbed.
- The two older three-board tables are kept as history and dated, saying which fixtures they predate and that a number should be re-measured before it is quoted.
- **The constant was not changed.** Moving it invalidates five ratchets and five measured bands, so it is its own piece of work with its own before-and-after rather than a line edited while writing a table.

- **The gain sits entirely on the two boards the value would have been fitted on.** `stm32_breakout` and `multi_ic` are the pair that wanted 2 in the original three-board sweep. Every fixture added since - `shift_driver` 33 -> 38 shorts, `qfp_fanout` 147 -> 186, `plane_board` 18 -> 24 - is worse at 2, and so is `led_blink`. Four against two, and the two chose the value.
- **`led_blink` gains its first short and it is not a near miss:** `D1 <-> via 'GND': Clearance violation: 0.00mm actual`. A via touching a foreign pad on the simplest board in the project. By this project's own ranking that outweighs violation counts elsewhere.

The before-and-after table is now in `docs/routing.md` and the instrument is in the dropped table, the second one there to be dropped twice.

Seventeen instruments have now been measured and dropped; `docs/routing.md` has said for several fires that the next real gain is a cost model rather than another constant, and two failed attempts at this one are evidence for that rather than against it.

The only command that touched the importer was `parse-kicad`, which prints metadata as JSON.

| `cypcb check led_blink.kicad_pcb` | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| edge-clearance | 5 | **0** |
| unrouted-pin | 12 | **8** |
| clearance | 0 | 3, one of them a 0.00mm short |

- DONE: **the loop closes - draw a board in KiCad, route it here, open it in KiCad.** `route` takes a `.kicad_pcb` and writes one back. The `.cypcb` path appends trace blocks to a copy of the source, and doing that to a `(kicad_pcb ...)` file would have produced something neither reader can open, so the KiCad input gets its own writer.
- **What is written is narrow on purpose:** the `(segment ...)` and `(via ...)` forms routing produces, inserted before the file's own closing paren. Footprints, setup, nets, zones this importer would not approximate - everything the project models loosely or not at all - is carried through byte for byte. The safest way to preserve what you do not model is not to rewrite it.
