- **The stacked vias were chased and the obvious fix was measured and dropped.** After routing: `stm32_breakout` 4 hole-to-hole, `multi_ic` 7, `qfp_fanout` 15, most of them reading as a net against itself at 0.00mm.
- The plausible cause - a net's paths are converted to vias separately, so two paths changing layer at one point each ask for one - is **not** the cause. The drill files settle it: at (56.134, 41.910) one via goes into the `Top-In1` pass and the other into the through pass, so they have different layer spans and are repeats of nothing.
- Measured anyway, since the filter is four lines: deduplicating by position and span moved `qfp_fanout` from 309 violations to 291 and left **every hole-to-hole count identical**, 4, 7 and 15 before and after. It removes something, and that something is not what it was written for. Reverted - a change whose stated reason does not hold is one nobody can maintain, and 18 violations are not worth carrying a false explanation.
- Written up in `docs/routing.md` as the eighteenth instrument measured and dropped, with what a real fix would have to do: stop the search putting a via where the board already has one at any depth, which is a cost-model question rather than a filter on the output.
- DONE: **the cost model already has a knob for the stacked holes, and it is the wrong lever.** `CongestionMap` tracks the cells each via's ring covers and charges `ring_penalty` per ring; the default is **0.0**, so the search knows where every hole is and pays nothing to put another on top. That looked like the whole answer.
- Swept at 0, 1, 3 and 8 on the three fixtures that stack holes, with violations and hole-to-hole measured together in one run. **No price wins on both counts, and none wins on either consistently**: `stm32_breakout` improves at 8 (180 -> 158 violations, 4 -> 1 holes), `multi_ic` gets worse at stacking at every price tried (7 -> 13, 8, 12), and `qfp_fanout` halves its stacked holes at 1 while paying 67 violations, outside its band of 57.
- **The reason is what the penalty charges for.** A ring price makes the search avoid *crossing* copper around an existing via; it says nothing about *placing* a via on a cell that already has one. On a crowded board it pushes routes away from rings and creates the congestion that makes another layer change attractive somewhere else. Nineteenth instrument measured and dropped; the sweep stays as a diagnostic.
- Recorded with it: the 27 stacked holes this sweep reports for `qfp_fanout` and the 15 from `drc_report` are the same board through different harnesses - one checks against `DesignRules::jlcpcb_2layer`, the other against the `jlcpcb` preset - which do not share a hole-to-hole minimum. Rows compare within a table, never across.
- DONE: **`CELL_VIA` was never set because it cannot be**, and that is a hard constraint on the cost-model work rather than an oversight. `is_free` reads `self.layers[layer][idx] == CELL_FREE` - an equality against zero - so any bit set in a cell's byte is a hard veto. A flag written purely to record something blocks the cell that carries it.
- Measured rather than reasoned: recording each via on the layers it spans, with **nothing reading the flag**, moved every board. `qfp_fanout` 309 violations -> **383** and `plane_board` 28 -> 29, both past their ratchets; `multi_ic` 291 -> 222 and `shift_driver` 65 -> 49 the other way. A change that only writes a note should not have a before and after at all, and the ratchets caught the claim that it did not.
- Reverted; all six ratchets back at their committed values. Written up in `docs/routing.md` beside the two instruments already dropped chasing these holes.
- **Where the memory has to live instead:** beside `CongestionMap`'s ring array, which already carries per-cell counts the search reads as *cost* rather than as *permission*. That is the difference between the two structures, and it is the whole reason one of them can hold this and the other cannot.
- DONE and reverted: **the fourth attempt, built exactly where the third said it had to go.** `CongestionMap` gained a `holes` count beside `ring`, marked when a net's path is committed and unmarked on rip-up, read by the search as `via_stack_penalty` per hole at the one moment a via is *placed*. At 0.0 it reproduced every fixture byte for byte, which is the right way to add a knob.
- **At 5, 20 and 100 it also reproduced every fixture byte for byte** - identical violations, shorts, stacked holes, vias and routes. A term that costs a hundred and changes nothing is never charged, and I did not establish why before the budget ran out. The likely reading, recorded for whoever picks it up: a net's holes are marked only once all its paths are committed, so same-net stacking - `VCC_3V3` against `VCC_3V3`, most of these violations - cannot see itself.
- Reverted rather than shipped. A knob that provably does nothing is worse than no knob: it reads like a lever, moves nothing, and costs the next person a fire to discover that.
- Four attempts now, each narrowing the next, all in `docs/routing.md` with numbers: not the output filter, not the ring price, not the occupancy byte, and not this shape of hole count until the marking moment is understood.
- **One of the two candidates for the dead knob is eliminated, by reading rather than by rebuilding.** `variant.rs` copies seven `AutorouteConfig` fields and ends `..AutorouteConfig::default()`, which looked like the answer - anything a caller sets outside those seven is replaced. It is not: `via_price_sweep` sets `via_foreign_copper_penalty`, which is not among the seven, calls `route_board` directly, and gets a real spread of 33 to 42. The sweep that found nothing took the same route, so the plumbing carried the value.
- The seven-field copy is **not a defect either**, which is worth recording so nobody else chases it: what it drops falls back to the shipped defaults, and those are the measured values. The CLI has only two paths - `--fast` with plain defaults, or variants - and neither loses a tuned setting.
- So the remaining candidate is the marking moment: a net's rings, and the holes marked beside them, are recorded only once all of that net's paths are committed. That would explain same-net stacking not seeing itself; it does not explain the cross-net pairs, so it may not be the whole answer.
- **The cause is still not established, and this fire says so rather than guessing again.** My previous commit published the marking-time reading as "the most likely"; that was one candidate of two presented as if it were the finding, and the doc now says what is known and what is not.
- DONE: **instrumented instead of rebuilding, and the second candidate falls too.** Counting how often the via-transition branch prices a layer change at a cell already covered by a via ring: `multi_ic` **46,181 of 2,836,140** evaluations (1.63%), `qfp_fanout` **49,376 of 1,783,840** (2.77%).
- Tens of thousands of times per board the search evaluates putting a via where one already is, **with that information in front of it**. The congestion map holds it at the right moment, so the marking is not too late and the idea is not unworkable.
- **The fourth attempt therefore failed on its own wiring, not on principle.** A price at that decision point can work; what it needs first is a check that the hole array is actually populated - one assertion after routing one fixture, which the fourth attempt never made before trusting its sweep.
- It also explains the ring price: it charges all 46,181 of those evaluations for *crossing* copper, which is why it moved every board, and nothing extra for stacking, which is why it moved no stacked hole.
- Probe reverted; no code change. Four attempts, two eliminated causes, and the question is now narrow enough to be worth a fifth.
- DONE: **the fifth attempt found the bug, measured the price, and the price does not pay.**
- **The fourth attempt's bug was one line.** `congestion_map.set_stack_penalty(..)` was never added beside `set_ring_penalty` - my edit had matched no text and I never checked - so the map's penalty stayed 0.0 and `stacking_cost` returned zero however high the knob went. A price of 100 producing byte-identical boards was exactly that.
- Rebuilt with the check first, which is the lesson: routing `multi_ic` leaves **364 holes recorded for 119 vias**, about three layers each, so the map is populated *before* a price is swept against it.

| stack price | stm32_breakout | multi_ic | qfp_fanout |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 (shipped) | 180 / 4 | 291 / 7 | 309 / 27 |
| 5 | 208 / **0** | 245 / 15 | 368 / 31 |
| 20 | 184 / 2 | **237** / 9 | 366 / 31 |
| 100 | 203 / 1 | 237 / 9 | 371 / 30 |

- Violations then stacked holes, read against the bands 59, 65 and 57: `stm32_breakout` clears its stacking at 5 and gives back 28 violations; `multi_ic` is 54 violations better at 20 and *worse* at stacking; `qfp_fanout` is worse on both at every price. **No price wins.**
- **Kept at 0.0 rather than reverted**, unlike the fourth attempt, and the difference is that this one demonstrably works - every nonzero price moves the boards, the shipped default reproduces the router exactly, and a future sweep is one command. Same basis `via_ring_penalty` is kept on.
- NEXT-ACTION: none in this vector. Five attempts, and the honest summary is that stacked holes are not reachable by pricing the placement either - the two boards that improve and the one that worsens disagree in a way no single constant resolves, the same shape as the pad-zone margin. The next real move is a rule that varies with the board, and nothing here has established what it would key on.

### V3 - `cypcb-desktop`, the workspace member nothing compiles
- DONE: **the AppImage failure has a root cause now, it is nine lines of a vendored script, and it is not this project's code.** Tauri reports `failed to run linuxdeploy` and nothing else; every step of this came from running the tool by hand and then reading the plugin it runs.
- **Where it stops.** `/config/.cache/tauri/linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk.sh`, lines 300-310. After setting rpaths it walks three module directories - GTK's immodules and printbackends, and gdk-pixbuf's loaders - and symlinks every `.so` in them flat into `$APPDIR/usr/lib`:

  ```
  for directory in "${PATCH_ARRAY[@]}"; do
      while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
          ln $verbose -s "${file/\/usr\/lib\//}" "$APPDIR/usr/lib"
      done < <(find "$directory" -name '*.so' -print0)
  done
  ```

  `ln -s` without `-f` fails when the name is taken, the script exits 1, and linuxdeploy reports `Failed to run plugin: gtk`.
- **Measured, on an AppDir the same build had just created from nothing.** The three directories hold 13, 2 and 12 `.so` files and share **no basename between them** - `uniq -d` over all 27 is empty, so they are not colliding with each other. `$APPDIR/usr/lib/` already contains `im-am-et.so`, `im-broadway.so`, `im-cedilla.so` and the rest of the immodules by the time the loop runs, put there by linuxdeploy's own dependency copying earlier in the same invocation. The plugin then tries to link the same names in again.

- **Nothing is changed here on the strength of it.** The one-character fix is `ln -sf` in a file that lives in a download cache and is fetched again whenever it is missing, so patching it would work once and mislead afterwards. It belongs upstream, in `linuxdeploy-plugin-gtk`.
- **The practical position is comfortable**, which is why this is recorded rather than worked around: `target/release/bundle/deb/CodeYourPCB_0.1.0-beta_amd64.deb` and `.../rpm/CodeYourPCB-0.1.0-beta-1.x86_64.rpm` are real, 7.3MB each, and a Linux user installs either. Only the AppImage is missing.

### V2 - Autorouter and routing quality
- DONE: **the action about teaching the router to lay a neck was written on a false premise, and checking it first turned up a real loss one step further on.** The seventh stale action in this project, and the third I wrote myself.
- **The router never sees a neck, because a net cannot declare one.** `neck` is a `trace` directive and nothing else: `NetConstraints` carries `width`, `clearance`, `current` and `impedance` and no neck, so there is no path by which autorouted copper could carry one. And a `trace` block already joins the pins, so the router lays nothing on that net - measured, not reasoned: `cypcb route --in-house` on a design with `trace SIG { from R1.2 to R2.1 width 2mm neck 0.8mm for 4mm }` reports **0 segments, 0 vias**.
- **What the check turned up instead: a necked trace did not survive being written down.** `board_as_dsl` emitted the layer, the width, the path and the lock, and **not the neck**. The file looked right - the split vertex the neck put in the geometry was still there, at 25.5mm on a 10.5-to-29.5 run - so a reader would not have suspected it. On reload the thin stretch is drawn *from the declaration*, and a file with the geometry and no declaration comes back as uniform copper at the full width. Fixed, and the writer reads the neck in the same query as the trace rather than in a second pass paired by iteration order.
- **The stale binary nearly produced a false finding.** The first run of that experiment showed a path with two points and no split, which reads as `apply_neck` not running on the `from`/`to` shape. `./target/release/cypcb` predated the morning's commit; the crate had been rebuilt and the CLI had not. **Rebuild the binary you are about to make a claim from.**
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-world --test a_neck_survives_being_written_down` -> **3 passed**, including reading the written file back and getting the same 4mm of thin copper. Mutation: the `neck` line removed from the writer -> **2 failed**. `./target/release/cypcb route /tmp/neckdemo.cypcb --in-house --fast -o -` -> `0 segments, 0 vias` and a trace block carrying `neck 0.800000mm for 4.000000mm`. `cargo test --workspace --exclude cypcb-desktop` -> clean. `cargo test -p cypcb-autoroute --release --test benchmark_validation -- --ignored` -> 2 passed, ratchets unmoved. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- NEXT-ACTION (**stale, done in `919b081`**: a net can declare `neck` and the router applies it; the live thread is in V5): **a net cannot say it wants to neck, and the owner's own example was a net.** The request recorded in `a_neck_says_how_far_it_runs.rs` is `netclass Mains [current 10A]` - a netclass, giving a trace millimetres wide, on a 2.54mm pitch. The feature landed on `trace` only, so the case that prompted it still cannot be written. The change is a language one and it is the whole width of the stack: `neck` as a net constraint in `grammar.js` and both readers, a field on `NetConstraints`, carried through `sync`, and applied to the finished route in `apply_routes` the way `sync_ast_to_world` applies it to a drawn one. Do the reader and the model first and leave the router for a second commit - `RoutingResult` groups by `(net_id, layer)` there, so the net is in hand and `Trace::apply_neck` is one call per trace whose net declares one.

- DONE: **the language draws the neck it declares.** `neck 0.8mm for 4mm` was a note beside a trace that ran 2mm the whole way; it is 4mm of 0.8mm copper now, and the check added yesterday can read it on a board written here rather than only on copper from the router or a KiCad file.
- **`Trace::apply_neck` narrows the last `neck.length` of the run and cuts the segment the boundary falls inside**, so the join is where the width changes rather than wherever a vertex happened to be. The cut point is interpolated in i128 - a long segment on a large board would overflow the multiply in i64.
- **The far end is the necked end, and that is a decision rather than a measurement.** A `trace ... from A to B` is written in the direction it runs and the thin copper is there because the pad it arrives at has no room for the wide copper. Written down in the doc comment as a choice so nobody has to reverse-engineer it from the geometry.
- **Two declarations are deliberately not drawn**: a neck no narrower than the trace, and a neck longer than the trace. Both are faults `NeckDownRule` already reports, and drawing either would turn a reported fault into geometry that hides it - a segment stating the width it already has, or a trace that is all neck and reports nothing thin.
- **One reader for both shapes.** A `trace` is built in two places, from a `path` and from `from`/`to`, and `declared_neck` is called by both. A neck drawn on one shape and not the other is the kind of difference nobody finds until a board is wrong.
- **A test in that file had to be rewritten rather than kept passing.** `a_declared_neck_with_no_thin_copper_is_not_reported` said "what the language produces today: one width for the whole trace", which stopped being true in this commit. It now builds that case directly - uniform KiCad copper under a design that states a neck - because the case is still real and the reason it was reachable is not.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test a_neck_says_how_far_it_runs` -> **13 passed**, up from 11, including `the_language_draws_the_neck_it_declares` asserting 4mm of necked length, a cut segment, 2mm at the near end and 0.8mm at the far one. `cargo test -p cypcb-world --doc trace` -> 16 passed. It writes `trace.width_at(index)` now, which answers the trace's width for every segment stating none - so a board that really is one width end to end is written exactly as before.

This one compares `Trace::necked_length()` - how far the segments really run thin - against the declared `for <length>`, and reports `the copper runs thin for 6mm where the neck allows 4mm: the declaration is not what was drawn`. Its module doc no longer says the necked stretch is not in the segments; that sentence came out in the same commit as the check that replaced it.
- **A declared neck with no thin copper is not a violation, and there is a test that says so.** The language cannot draw a neck yet - a `trace` states one width and one neck, and every segment it syncs to runs at the trace's width - so the fourth check has nothing to measure on a board written in the language. Reading zero thin millimetres as "the trace overran" would have failed every design that uses the feature.

After that, the router: `pathfinder_v2.rs` reads a net's width and knows nothing about necks, so it cannot lay one, and a design that states a neck is routed without it.

- DONE: **the same defect was alive in the viewer, in four places, and the fix for it came with a test that proved nothing until it was rewritten.** `f7c1b28` wired `ruleset_for_world` into `cypcb route` and `cypcb score` and recorded that `cypcb-render` builds `PresetRuleSet::new` four times. All four are production - `auto_route`, `auto_route_with_params`, `auto_route_debug`, `auto_route_variants` - so the editor's own router ignored the constraints the command line had just started obeying. Same board, same design, two behaviours depending on which of the two you routed from.
- **The first test written for it was vacuous, and the mutation is what said so.** It stated `net VCC [width 0.4mm]`, routed through `PcbEngine`, and asserted the emitted width. It passed. Reverting all four sites to `PresetRuleSet::new` -> **46 passed**, unchanged. The reason is the one this vector already recorded: `pathfinder_v2.rs:174` reads `world.net_constraints(net).width` directly and never consults the rule set, so a width assertion cannot tell the two apart. `net_width_override.rs` has always passed for the same reason.
- **Rewritten to measure clearance, which has no second path.** Two engines, one board, the watched net saying nothing in the first and `[clearance 4mm]` in the second; route both, count traces and total copper, assert the two results differ. Reverting the four sites -> `assertion left != right failed: a net demanding 4mm of space routed identically to one that said nothing`, **1 failed**. The doc comment says which of the two it measures and why, so the next person does not re-write the width version.
- **A third instance of the same family, fixed in passing.** `auto_route_variants` scored every variant with `DesignRules::default()` - which is `jlcpcb_2layer`, and matched the preset above it only because that preset is hard-coded to `jlcpcb`. Now `DesignRules::from_constraints(&preset.constraints())`. Two coincidences agreeing is not one source.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-render --features native --lib` -> **46 passed**. Mutation, all four sites back to `PresetRuleSet::new` -> **1 failed**, named above. `cargo clippy -p cypcb-render --all-targets` clean. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- NEXT-ACTION: none in this vector beyond what `f7c1b28` already left - `current` is still not a width, for the layer reason recorded there. What this run adds to that entry is a warning about how to test it: an assertion about **width** cannot distinguish a wired rule set from an unwired one, because width reaches the trace by a second route. Any future test of a constraint reaching the router has to pick a constraint the rule set alone carries.

- DONE: **the router never received the clearance the design asked for, and nothing had noticed because nothing outside a unit test ever built a rule set with overrides in it.** `PresetRuleSet` has carried `with_overrides` and `set_net_override` since the presets were written; `grep -rn "set_net_override" crates/ --include=*.rs` finds three callers and all three are its own tests. Every real caller - `route.rs` twice, `score.rs` once, `cypcb-render` four times - built `PresetRuleSet::new(preset)`, which is the fab preset and nothing else. So the router planned against one set of numbers and `cypcb check` graded the result against another, the design's, and the gap surfaced as violations on a board the router thought it had finished.
- **Width was already carried and clearance was not, which is why this looked fine.** `pathfinder_v2.rs:174` reads `world.net_constraints(net.net_id)?.width?` directly, so `net VCC [width 0.4mm]` really was emitted at 0.4mm and `net_width_override.rs` really did pass. Nothing anywhere read `.clearance`. The width path also stops short of the grid: `grid.rs:196` bloats obstacles by `min_clearance + min_trace_width / 2` from the **rule set**, so a wide net was drawn wide and planned as if it were minimum width.
- **New `cypcb_drc::ruleset_for_world(preset, world)`**, in the one crate that has the world, the rules and the calculator together. It reads each net's stated width and clearance out of the registry and raises the preset's two figures to them. Raises only: a design asking for copper thinner than the fabricator images is a fault `MinTraceWidthRule` reports, not licence to plan below what can be made. Nets the design says nothing about are absent from the map and route exactly as before.
- **Measured on `examples/mains-sequencer.cypcb`, which is the board the owner raised this from** - `netclass Mains [current 10A clearance 3mm]`. Before: 768 segments, 55 vias, and `cypcb check` reporting **462 clearance violations**, 58 trace-current, 5 shorts, 0 unrouted pins. After: 319 segments, 29 vias, **199 clearance**, 62 trace-current, **122 shorts, 84 unrouted pins**. That is not an improvement and is not written as one. The board is not manufacturable either way; what changed is that the router now attempts the 3mm the design states instead of routing to 0.2mm and being graded at 3mm. The mains rule on this board, at this board size, is beyond the router.
- **A second fault the change exposed rather than caused.** `route_variants` scored every variant with `DesignRules::from_constraints(constraints_for_net(rules, 0))` - net **0**, whichever net that happens to be, used as a stand-in for the preset. That was harmless only while no net had an override. On this board a mains net interns first, so every variant would have been scored against 3mm. Now `rules.preset().constraints()`. Evidence it was live: the composites moved uniformly the moment it was fixed, `PathFinder Default` 320053.0 -> 300053.0 and `Guarded Pads` 219052.8 -> 204052.8, with the same routes underneath.
- **The six benchmark boards do not move, and the reason is structural rather than lucky.** `set_net_constraints` is called from `sync.rs` only - the DSL path - so a KiCad-imported board has no stated constraints, the override map is empty, and `with_overrides(preset, {})` is `new(preset)`. Confirmed by running them: `cargo test -p cypcb-autoroute --release --test benchmark_validation -- --ignored` -> **2 passed**, every ratchet held, stm32_breakout 187 against 239, multi_ic 304 against 356, shift_driver 65 against 82, qfp_fanout 318 against 366, plane_board 28 against 28, all with 0 unrouted.
- **One-sided, and the module says so rather than leaving it to be found.** `ClearanceRule` folds a pair of nets with `.max` (`clearance.rs:150`), so mains-to-signal is 3mm measured from either end. A rule set is consulted per net being routed, so the mains net is planned at 3mm and a signal approaching it afterwards is still planned at the preset.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --lib net_rules` -> **4 passed**. Mutation, making `wider` return the floor unconditionally -> **2 failed**. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- NEXT-ACTION: **`current` is still not a width, and the reason is the layer.** `netclass Mains [current 10A]` needs IPC-2221, which `cypcb-calc` has and `TraceCurrentRule` already uses - but the answer depends on whether the copper lands on an outer layer, which sheds heat into the air, or an inner one, which does not. The rule set is built before the router picks a layer. `current_alone_is_not_yet_a_width` pins the present behaviour so the choice is made deliberately: plan every current-bearing net at the inner-layer width and over-build the outer ones, or make the rule set answer per layer. The second is the honest one and is a change to `RoutingRuleSet`, not to this module.

- **The resolution is to use each structure for what it knows.** The field gives a distance and no net, and is right outside the zone. `pad_owner` gives a net and no distance, is already per-cell, and is right inside it. So inside a pad zone the barrier is narrowed rather than switched off: it applies to cells whose `pad_owner` is a **different** net and to nothing else. A route stays free to reach its own pin and keeps paying for a stranger's pad it is sitting on.

Proven on a two-net board: VCC comes out at 0.4mm on every segment and the net that says nothing keeps the 0.127mm preset. The benchmark fixtures are KiCad imports and declare nothing, so 0/167/110 is unchanged.

Read the code before writing the next action from memory.
- DONE: **the benchmark DRC numbers now say who caused them.** The fixtures are KiCad boards with parts already placed, so a violation in the routed board might be one the router made or one the import brought with it, and nothing distinguished the two. `drc_report` runs DRC twice - once on the fixture as imported, once after routing - and lists only what appears in the second run. Measured: led_blink 0 before / 0 after, stm32_breakout **3 before / 176 after / 173 introduced**, multi_ic **5 before / 127 after / 122 introduced**. The router is responsible for essentially all of them; blaming the fixtures would have been comfortable and wrong.
- ~~NEXT-ACTION: refine the clearance narrow phase to actual pads and add a courtyard rule~~ **Done.** `ClearanceRule::component_pads` measures per-pad copper with per-pad nets, `CourtyardClearanceRule` keeps placement collisions reported, and both are registered - `crates/cypcb-drc/src/rules/courtyard_clearance.rs` exists and `lib.rs` boxes it. This line stood after the work landed, which is how a fresh session picks up an action that is already finished.
- DONE: **a probe that says which half of the router to blame.** `tests/grid_vs_checker.rs` (`--ignored`) takes every clearance violation the router introduces, maps its coordinate onto the grid the router used, and reports what that cell was marked as - a route through a cell marked `CELL_PAD` means the search ignores its own obstacles, a violation on a free cell means the marking never happened. Cross-tabbed against the shape of the pair, stm32_breakout's 103: **trace-via 66 (64 of them on free cells)**, trace-trace 33 (18 on pad cells), via-via 3, part-via 1. multi_ic's 28: trace-trace 23 (20 on pad cells), trace-via 3, part 2. Grids are 296x256 at 0.254mm and 197x158 at 0.508mm per cell.
- **Failed experiment, measured, do not repeat: hard-owning the via ring in the grid.** The finding above has an obvious reading - a via's copper is never written into the grid at all, only into the congestion map, where it is a price a later net can pay rather than a fact it must respect. Marking the ring as the net's own copper (`mark_route` over `via_footprint_cells`) made both boards worse: stm32_breakout **124 -> 154** introduced (clearance 103 -> 125, hole-to-hole 3 -> 9, routes 858 -> 965), multi_ic **42 -> 55** (clearance 28 -> 38). Reverted, and the revert re-measured back to 124 / 42 exactly. This is the third time a hard block has cost more than it bought. The reason is arithmetic: the via keepout is `drill/2 + annular + clearance + width/2` = 0.15 + 0.127 + 0.127 + 0.0635 = 0.4675mm, which at 0.254mm per cell rounds up to a 2-cell disc - 0.508mm, nearly double the ring's actual 0.277mm of copper. At this resolution the grid cannot express via clearance without over-blocking. The honest routes are a finer grid near vias, or a post-route repair driven by real DRC output.
- **The repair pass currently buys nothing, and the tracker said otherwise.** `route_board` runs `strategy.route` and then `repair_routes`; the benchmark diagnostics called `strategy.route` directly, so they measured a router the product never ships alone. Pointed at `route_board` they report **exactly the same numbers** - 858 routes / 124 introduced and 1027 / 42, identical to the un-repaired path on all three fixtures. Repair therefore accepts no attempt on any of them today. The 176 -> 167 and 127 -> 110 recorded below were measured before the clearance rule was fixed, and no longer describe this code.

### V3 - Build, CI and quality gates
- DONE: **`cypcb-fixtures`: a board whose layers cannot be mistaken for one another.** Three index errors have shipped here and every one was found by a mutation or by running the binary, never by the test meant to cover it - the outer layers reading the dielectric on the wrong side, `BottomCopper` read as copper entry 0, and `Layer::Inner(0)` read as entry 0 rather than 1. All three had one cause: **a symmetric stack gives neighbouring layers the same answer**, so a rule reading the wrong index produces the right number and the test passes.
- **The fixture separates the four layers by their foil, not by their surroundings.** 0.035, 0.0175, 0.025 and 0.07mm with 0.1mm of the same laminate between every pair. Uniform dielectrics on purpose: what makes the four answers differ is then the layer itself, so a test asserting one is asserting the layer it asked about rather than a difference in the material around it. Both inner layers stay genuinely centred, because "this layer has no answer" and "this layer has the wrong answer" are different failures and this fixture is for the second.
- **A crate rather than a helper in one of them.** `cypcb-world` and `cypcb-drc` had each built their own symmetric stack, and the next rule that reads a layer index would have built a third. It is a dev-dependency of both and `publish = false`, so nothing that ships links it.
- **Both consumers assert the fixture's own promise**, which is the part that would otherwise rot quietly: `cypcb-world` checks each copper entry answers with its own foil and that the inner two are striplines while the outer two are not; `cypcb-drc` runs the rule on all four layers and fails if any two report the same impedance. A fixture that loses this property stops catching what it was built for, and every test resting on it goes quiet with it.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-world --test where_a_copper_layer_sits` -> **8 passed**; `-p cypcb-drc --test what_the_stack_delivers_against_what_the_net_asked_for` -> **9 passed**. Mutations on the fixture itself, each run against **both** suites and reverted: the two inner foils made equal -> 1 failed in each; the two outer foils made equal -> 1 failed in each; an inner layer's centring broken -> 1 failed in each. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- **A markdown substring replace damaged a heading and the gate caught it.** Inserting the new section before `## cypcb-world` matched the last two hashes of `### cypcb-world`, leaving a level-two heading and attributing its dependencies to the new crate. `the_architecture_names_the_workspace` failed on both halves at once. Same family as the string-offset cut that destroyed two functions earlier in this project: **anchor on a line, not on a substring.**

Those two are warnings now, everything else stays an error. Both fixes mutation-checked: severity forced back to `"error"` fails `a_board_being_written_is_not_an_error`, the span lookup forced to `None` fails `a_diagnostic_points_at_the_part_it_names` with the 0,0 range quoted above.

Completion on a line still being typed did not: `component R3 resistor "` with the string open is unparseable, so the AST held no such component, `find_completion_context` read the cursor as "after the last definition" and returned the **top-level keywords** - the editor offered `version`, `board`, `net`, `module`, `assert` inside a footprint string, where accepting one pastes a whole snippet into the string.
- **The cause is that the context came from the AST alone, and a half-written definition is exactly what a parser cannot return.** The context now falls back to the text under the cursor, and only when the AST placed the cursor nowhere: an odd number of quotes on the line means the cursor is inside a string, and `component` as the line's first word makes it a footprint name; otherwise the innermost unclosed `{` is found - skipping braces inside strings - and its opening line names the block. `component`/`board`/`net`/`footprint` bodies offer their own properties.
- Both halves mutation-checked: with the fallback returning `None`, `completion_works_on_the_half_typed_line_it_is_asked_about` and `completion_inside_a_block_nobody_has_closed_yet_offers_its_properties` fail, the second with `["version", "board", "component", ...]` where `value` and `at` belong. The two that passed first time were checked too - `goto_definition` forced to `None` fails the definition test, `footprint_completions` forced empty fails both footprint tests - because a test that has never been red proves nothing.

- DONE: **the pin-to-pin trace was worse than the drift said, and the defect was in Rust.** Chasing the viewer's missing trace led to `get_pin_position` in `cypcb-world/src/sync.rs`, which returned the **component's own position** under a comment calling it "a good approximation" and a four-line list of what a complete version would do. So `trace VCC { from R1.1 to C1.1 }` was copper between two part centres, touching neither pad it names - and that copper is what the exporter writes into the Gerber. On `examples/syntax.cypcb` the segment ran 5mm to 20mm, the two part origins; it now runs **4.5mm to 19.5mm**, which is R1 pad 1 to C1 pad 1.
- The endpoint is the pad the reference names, offset by the footprint and turned by the part's rotation - the same transform `copper.rs` and `RoutingGrid::populate_pads` use, so the checker, the router and the writer agree on where a pad is. A footprint nobody registered or a pin it does not have falls back to the part's position rather than dropping the copper, because a missing pin is reported where the netlist is checked and a silently missing trace is the harder failure to notice.
- Proof: `crates/cypcb-world/tests/a_pin_to_pin_trace_lands_on_the_pads.rs`, three tests that compute the expected point from the library rather than repeating a number - the copper starts and ends on the named pads; a part turned 90 degrees moves its pad off the x axis and the copper follows; and a pin the footprint does not have still draws something. Workspace 1419 passed, clippy clean, viewer 178 passed.
- DONE: **the viewer draws pin-to-pin traces now, and it draws the same copper the CLI does.** `parseSource` read the `trace` block and produced no segment unless it carried a `path`, so `trace VCC { from R1.1 to C1.1 }` was invisible on screen while the exporter wrote it into the Gerber. It resolves both pads with the same transform the engine uses - the footprint's offset, turned by the part's rotation, added to the part's position - and resolves them **after** the whole file is read, so a trace may name a part written below it.
- **The check was strengthened before the entries were struck off, which is the part worth keeping.** `parser-drift.test.ts` compared trace *counts*; it compares the geometry now - net, layer, width and every endpoint in nanometres, with one spelling for a layer because the two sides print `TopCopper` and `Top`. Under that stricter comparison the four boards agree exactly, so the fix is a match rather than a coincidence of counts. `KNOWN_DRIFT` is down to the three module and import boards.
- Proof: `npx vitest run` -> 21 files, **178 passed**, with the drift test green only because the list shrank; `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` on both changed files silent.
- DONE: **V4's parser decision is costed and taken: route (b), a Rust reader.** `docs/one-parser.md` holds the measurement. Route (a) - a wasm C toolchain - has to build our generated `parser.c` **and the tree-sitter runtime, 13,647 lines of C across 13 files**, with clang against a wasm sysroot, while the engine targets `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, which has no libc; the sysroot that exists is `wasi-libc`, for `wasm32-wasip1`. And it buys nothing beyond parsing: the duplicate TypeScript reader would still be there, so modules and imports would still land twice, as the pin-to-pin trace just did.
- **The number that decided it: nothing consumes the concrete syntax tree.** Every caller - `cypcb-cli`'s five commands, `cypcb-lsp` (`document.rs` calls `parse()`), `cypcb-render`, `cypcb-world::sync` - takes the AST. So a reader that fills `ast.rs`'s 47 public types with correct spans serves the tooling unchanged, `imports.rs` and `errors.rs` are untouched, `parser.rs`'s 3,226 lines of CST-to-AST are **replaced rather than added to**, and `parseSource`'s 439 lines are deleted.
- The oracle is already in the repo, which is what makes this a project rather than a rewrite: `cypcb parse -o ast` prints today's AST as JSON, so a new reader is correct when it prints byte-identical JSON for every example. Order of work is in the doc, four steps, each shippable alone.
- DONE: **step 1 of the one-parser plan: a tokenizer and a reader in Rust, and it builds for wasm.** `crates/cypcb-parser/src/lexer.rs` (tokens: words, numbers, strings, punctuation, both comment forms) and `src/reader.rs` (recursive descent for `version`, `board`, `component`, `net`, `trace`), behind a `rust-parser` feature. Nothing in the shipping path calls it. The claim that matters is measured: `cargo build --release -p cypcb-parser --no-default-features --features rust-parser --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` **finishes**, where the tree-sitter path cannot without a wasm C toolchain.
- **It is checked against the parser it will replace, not against hand-written expectations.** `tests/differential.rs` reads every example both ways and compares the ASTs as JSON with spans stripped - tree-sitter's node boundaries and a hand-written reader's are not the same bytes, and pinning them now would pin tree-sitter's shape rather than the language's meaning. **80 definitions across 9 boards, identical.** The ten boards it does not claim are listed with the construct that skips them, and a test asserts each of those files exists, so the list stays honest as the reader grows.
- **Two guards, because two readers that both return nothing agree perfectly**: the test counts the definitions it compared and fails under 40, and the comparison was mutation-checked - making the reader ignore `locked` turns it red, and putting it back turns it green.

- DONE: **step 2 in one pass: the Rust reader covers every v1 construct.** `footprint` with its pads, courtyard and both silk forms; `zone` and `keepout`; `netclass` with the same constraint block a net carries; `outline`. The differential test went **80 definitions across 9 boards to 113 across 13**, all identical to what tree-sitter produces. `four-layer.cypcb` came off the skip list without any work - it was listed for a stackup it does not have, which is what a skip list costs when it is written from a guess rather than a run.
- What is left is the v2 four - `module`, `import`, `interface`, `assert` - plus the two boards written to fail parsing, where the question is error parity rather than coverage. Wasm still builds: `cargo build --release -p cypcb-parser --no-default-features --features rust-parser --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` -> `Finished`.
- DONE: **the Rust reader reads the whole language.** The v2 four landed together because they interlock: `module` with a body that holds the same definitions a design does, `use X as Y at ... rotate ... { PIN = net }`, `import` in both spellings, `interface`, and `assert` with comparisons, `within`, and all three tolerance forms. Typed values came with them - `value 10kohm` fills `typed_value` **and** the text, which is what the tree-sitter parser does and what anything that only prints a value needs.
- The lexer grew the operators the assertions need, longest-first so `>=` never reads as `>` then `=`.
- **The differential test now covers every example except the two written to fail parsing: 147 definitions across 17 boards, identical.** Mutation-checked on a v2 path: making the module instance accept a port without its `=` turns it red, putting it back turns it green. Wasm still builds; workspace 1419 passed; clippy clean.
- DONE: **step 1b, error parity - and measuring it found a real hole.** The reader skipped any word it did not recognise at the top level, which was correct while it was incomplete and wrong the moment it covered the language: `frobnicate 3` parsed clean, where tree-sitter reported it. A typo in a keyword meant a part quietly missing from the board and nothing said so. Unknown words are an error now, with the word in the message.
- `tests/error_parity.rs` pins both directions: five broken sources the language rejects and the reader must reject too, three good ones it must not reject, the repo's own two demonstration files, and the position - the reader's first error has to land within twenty bytes of tree-sitter's on the same fault, which it does. **What is not pinned is the count or the wording**: tree-sitter reports every token it could not place, this reader reports the first thing it wanted and walks to the next definition, so `unknown_keyword.cypcb` is two errors against one. Pinning those equal would pin a recovery strategy rather than a language.
- The gate runs it beside the differential test. Workspace 1419 passed, clippy clean.
- DONE: **step 3(a): the browser engine parses `.cypcb` itself, and the thing that stopped it was a feature line that was not true.** `cypcb-world`'s `sync` feature declared `cypcb-parser/tree-sitter-parser`, but `sync.rs` only ever uses `cypcb_parser::ast`, which every build of that crate has. That false dependency is what kept the AST-to-board path out of the browser. `sync = []` now, and `cypcb-render`'s `wasm` feature carries the Rust reader plus sync, so `PcbEngine::load_source` is exported to JS for the first time.
- **Measured, both columns**, on `viewer/build-wasm.sh` output: raw **751,995 -> 1,044,164 bytes**, gzipped **290,004 -> 411,147**. The artifact is clean - its 50 imports all come from the wasm-bindgen glue and **none from `env`**, which is what proves no C got linked in.
- Proof that the reader is really the one running: `crates/cypcb-render/tests/the_browser_build_reads_the_language.rs` builds with the browser's own features and asserts a board comes back with its parts, that **a module instance places both of its parts under the instance's name** - the exact defect the TypeScript reader has - and that `frobnicate 3` is still reported.
- DONE: **step 3(d), the half that matters: the browser reads `.cypcb` with the engine.** `WasmPcbEngineAdapter.load_source` called `parseSource` - the TypeScript reader - and shipped the result into the engine as a snapshot. It calls `wasmEngine.load_source(source)` now and reads the board back, so components, nets, traces, vias, zones, the copper the pours became, the ratsnest and the DRC violations all come from Rust. The trace-replay loop went with it: there is nothing left to hand back to an engine that already holds the model.
- **Verified where it counts, in a browser**: `npx playwright test` -> **93 passed, 0 failed, 17 skipped**, including the boards that load, render, toggle to 3D and report geometry. `npx tsc --noEmit` silent, `npx vitest run` 21 files and 178 passed.
- DONE: **the second reader is deleted.** `parseSource` and the helpers only it used - `parseUnit`, `getFootprintPads`, `getFootprintSilk`, `normalizePinName` - are gone, `viewer/src/wasm.ts` is 1,804 lines down to 1,210, and `MockPcbEngine.load_source` refuses with a sentence instead of parsing: a board that looks right and is not is worse than a build that says it has no engine. `zone-parsing.test.ts` and `parser-drift.test.ts` went with it - both existed to measure a reader that no longer exists, and what they covered is asserted in Rust.

What it buys is that a board using `module` or `import` now draws what the CLI exports, which is the defect the whole vector started from.
- Verified in a browser after the deletion: `npx playwright test` -> **93 passed, 0 failed, 17 skipped**. `npx vitest run` -> 19 files, 172 passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint src/wasm.ts` silent.
- DONE: **the native half of step 3: `parse` is the Rust reader everywhere, and no default build compiles C.** `rust-parser` is `cypcb-parser`'s default; the tree-sitter parser is `tree_sitter_parse` behind its own feature. The CLI's five commands lost `CypcbParser`, `cypcb-lsp` and `cypcb-render`'s native feature stopped asking for the C parser, and `imports.rs` moved to whichever reader the build has, since it only ever worked on the AST.
- **The proof is the absence**: `cargo tree --workspace -i tree-sitter` -> `package ID specification 'tree-sitter' did not match any packages`. The crate is not in the graph, so `build.rs` never runs `cc` and the fresh-clone story stops needing a C toolchain.
- The two comparison tests still need both parsers in one binary, so they build with `--features tree-sitter-parser` and the gate names them: `cargo test -p cypcb-parser --features tree-sitter-parser` -> **115 passed**, differential 147 definitions across 17 boards unchanged. The default workspace run is 1357 passed - lower than the 1434 before the flip because the tree-sitter parser's own unit tests only build with its feature, which is where they belong.

- DONE: **spans measured, and the risk was not there.** `tests/spans_point_at_the_source.rs` checks them against the thing that cannot drift - the source text: an identifier's span has to spell the identifier, a string's span has to be the quoted literal, a definition's span has to start with its keyword and contain everything inside it. All three hold on every example. Mutation-checked: moving an identifier's span one byte turns the first test red.
- **And the two parsers agree exactly.** The diagnostic in the same file compares definition spans between them: **147 identical, 0 different, widest gap 0 bytes.** The differential test strips spans by choice, not because they differ, and the LSP's hover and goto are reading the same offsets they always did.
- DONE: **measured where the router's cost model is blind, and the obvious answer is wrong.** `grid_vs_checker`, re-run today: the largest group of introduced clearance faults on both dense fixtures is a route's copper against a part's pad **on a cell the grid marked as a pad** - 109 of stm32_breakout's 206 mapped faults, 112 of multi_ic's 215. The obvious cause is the pad zone opening every pad a net has rather than the two a connection runs between.
- **Failed experiment, measured, reverted: opening only the connection's own two pads.** stm32_breakout 239 -> 299 after and 136 -> 175 shorts, multi_ic 336 -> 398 and 166 -> 219, with **nothing left unrouted** on either. So the router is not reaching through pads it has no business near; it is inside its own pad's disc, colliding with a **neighbouring part's** pad that the disc happens to cover. Eighth restriction tried in this vector, eighth to lose. Recorded in `docs/routing.md` with the reading it refutes.
- DONE: **a crate that only built inside the workspace now builds on its own.** The workspace declared `cypcb-parser = { ..., default-features = false }`, written when the default feature was the C parser and a wasm build had to opt out. With the reader as the default it means *no parser*, and `cargo clippy -p cypcb-autoroute --all-targets` failed on `cannot find function parse in crate cypcb_parser` while the whole-workspace run passed - feature unification was hiding it. The override is gone from the workspace and from `cypcb-drc`, `cypcb-world` and `cypcb-render`, and each of six crates now lints clean alone.
- DONE: **the radius was the suspect, and it pays.** The pad zone's radius had been the pad's own copper plus a flat three cells since the first version, under a comment reading "generous but safe" - 0.762mm on the 0.254mm grid, wider than the gap between the two pads of an 0402. Swept: **two cells beats three on both dense boards and both columns** - stm32_breakout 239 -> 216 violations and **136 -> 86 shorts**, multi_ic 336 -> 290 and 166 -> 131, all outside the noise bands this vector measured. Zero is not the floor: with no margin stm32_breakout leaves a connection unrouted and takes seven times as long.
- **It ships as a variant, not as the default, because led_blink goes the other way** - two near misses become one short, which is backwards under a ranking that puts shorts first. `PathFinder Tight Pads` is the eighth variant, and **stm32_breakout picks it in best-of-eight at 216 / 86** where its previous pick `Low-Via` gave 216 / 114. multi_ic keeps `Pad Aware`, led_blink keeps `High-Density`. The default path and the gate are untouched at 2/0, 239/136, 336/166.
- DONE: **named the fault that keeps the narrower opening out of the defaults, and refuted two fixes for it.** At margin 2 led_blink's new short is `D1 <-> via 'GND': 0.00mm` - a via whose ring lands on a part's pad, not a trace crossing one. Raising `pad_layer_change_penalty` (now a config knob rather than a constant) does not touch it: the short survives every price to 1000, and stm32_breakout gives back its win at 150 (216 -> 263). So the search is not choosing to pay - it never sees the fault.
- **And that is the finding worth keeping: `foreign_cells_in_via_keepout` counts `net_at` only.** That map holds routed copper; a pad's net lives in `pad_net`, because a rip-up clears `net_map` and a pad is not ripped up. **A via pays for landing its ring on another net's trace and nothing for landing it on another net's pad.** Measured directly: counting those cells at the shipped price of 0.25 takes stm32_breakout 239 -> 259 and multi_ic 336 -> 392 with 166 -> 216 shorts, because the keepout disc covers many pad cells on a dense board. Reverted - the blind spot is real, the price for it is not that one.
- DONE: **the blind spot is closed, the mechanism is confirmed, and it still does not earn a place in the defaults.** Pads inside a via's keepout are counted apart from routed copper now and priced by `via_foreign_pad_penalty`. At the narrower opening it does exactly what the theory said: led_blink's via-on-a-pad short **disappears at every price from 0.02 up**, taking that board from 2 violations with 1 short to **1 with 0** - better than the shipped default. The dense boards do not follow: stm32_breakout goes 216 / 86 to 272 / 147 at 0.02 and 239 / 124 at 0.05, multi_ic 290 / 131 to 277 / 121 at 0.02 and 330 / 168 at 0.05.
- **So it ships at zero.** No opening and price together beat what each board already picks in best-of-eight - stm32_breakout 216 / 86 from `Tight Pads`, multi_ic 267 / 106 from `Pad Aware`, led_blink 1 / 0 from `High-Density`. The knob is there, the numbers are in `docs/routing.md`, and what is missing is a board that wants it.
- DONE: **the command line stopped shipping the router's second-best answer.** `cypcb route --in-house` routed once with the default settings; `--variants` - best of eight, which the viewer has always done - was a flag nobody would know to pass. Measured on `examples/blink.cypcb`: one run gives **9 violations with 6 shorts**, best-of-eight gives **5 with 3**, for 0.9s against 0.06s. Best-of-eight is what `--in-house` does now, and `--fast` is there for when the wait matters more than the board.
- **And the coverage test that was supposed to catch a variant going missing did not check the last two.** `default_variant_configs_cover_the_measured_settings` asserts a variant prices via rings and guards pad keepouts; it now also asserts one prices a foreign pad (multi_ic picks it at 267/106) and one narrows the pad opening (stm32_breakout picks it at 216/86). A list nobody checks is a list a refactor quietly shortens.
- - NEXT-ACTION: none in this vector worth its cost. Eleven instruments have now been measured on these three fixtures; the two that pay are in the defaults, three are variants a board picks, and the rest are in the dropped table with the numbers that killed them. **The next real gain is a cost model rather than another knob**, and the evidence for that is this fire: every knob left moves one board and gives it back on another. Next fires should go elsewhere - V1's CLI surface and V5's roadmap features are both untouched for a dozen fires.

- DONE: **the flake had a name, and then a cause: 39 leftover dev servers.** Two gate runs had failed and passed on their own; the stage learned to print names last fire, and this time it did - `the-dev-server-guards-the-disk`, at `refuses to read a file outside it` with **`expected 'the private key' to be undefined`**. The browser has had hot reload since the dev server was written; a terminal had nothing.

Draining the queue did not help, because the events keep arriving rather than sitting in it. The command remembers what each file held when it last checked it, and a file whose bytes have not moved is not a save whatever the operating system says: **one edit, one check**, measured at 24 -> 27 -> 30 violations across two appends.

The badge is now required, and so is the word `clearance` in the panel. That second assertion is the one that matters: moving the two parts from 0.5mm to 25mm apart **still shows the badge** (unconnected pins are violations too), so badge visibility alone never proved a clearance check ran.

- Where it has to be looked for, because every interactive trace makes this journey: `engine.add_trace` puts it in the world, `syncTracesToEditor` replaces the whole managed section of the editor with `engine.export_traces_as_dsl()`, the editor's own 300ms debounce then fires `loadDesign(content)` - which **clears the world and parses the text again**. So a trace exists in copper only for as long as the DSL writer can spell it. Anything the writer cannot express is gone on the next keystroke, and nothing says so: `dsl.rs` already documents one such gap, a via's outer diameter, which is rebuilt from a default rather than read.

Then drive the interactive router from the end-to-end suite - two traces, three traces, a trace on each layer, one with a via, one whose segments do not chain, one on a net whose name needs quoting - and see which of them does not survive being written down and read back. The owner's report is two occurrences with no pattern yet; the instrument is what turns that into a cause.

- **Owner request, 2026-08-11: neck-down, and a way to reach it that is not typing.** Raised from the same session: on a mains board `netclass Mains [current 10A]` gives a trace several millimetres wide, correctly, and a 2.54mm pad pitch has nowhere to put it. Arriving at a pad, the copper reaches the neighbouring pad and DRC fires - which is the checker being right and the design having no way to say what every other EDA lets you say: that the last few millimetres before a pad may be narrower, because a short length of thin copper does not have time to heat.
- Three levels, and only the first exists today:
  1. **Two `trace` blocks, one wide and one narrow.** Works now, says nothing about intent, and the checker cannot tell a deliberate neck from a mistake.
  2. **`neck 0.8mm for 4mm` inside a trace** - the width and the length it is allowed to run at it, so the rule can be checked rather than trusted.
  3. **`netclass Mains [current 10A neck 0.8mm within 5mm of pad]`** - declared once, applied at every pad approach, and DRC reports it as a stated neck rather than as a violation.
- DRC needs a fourth thing with it: a violation category that means "narrower than the current asks for, and said so" rather than a clearance failure. Otherwise level 3 trades one wrong report for another.
- **And it must be clickable.** The owner's words: a Sims-style menu - right-click a trace or a pad and get the choices on the spot, neck, width, layer, delete, rather than going to the text for something you are doing with the mouse. The language stays the record; the menu is how you reach it while routing. `interaction.ts` already carries the routing keys - F flip layer, / posture, Q corner mode, A angle snap - so the actions exist and have no surface.
- NEXT-ACTION: **level 2 first**, because it is the smallest thing that makes a necked trace legal and checkable, and everything above it needs somewhere to write the result. The radial menu comes after, since it is a way of reaching syntax that has to exist first.

### V4 - Architecture and deduplication
- DONE: **the impedance test's two stacks were the fixture crate's two stacks, written out again.** `what_the_stack_delivers_against_what_the_net_asked_for` declared `ORDINARY` as a `Spec` table that is byte for byte `an_inner_layer_the_forms_cannot_describe`, and `CENTRED` as a symmetric all-prepreg stack the crate did not have. The duplicate is gone and the missing one is now `cypcb_fixtures::a_stack_that_answers_on_every_layer`, so the crate holds both of the stacks this project reasons about. One stack stays local: the lopsided one, which exists for a single assertion about reading the bottom face as the top.
- **The wiring was checked rather than assumed.** Thickening the fixture's prepreg from 0.2mm to 0.25mm -> **5 of 11 failed**; restored -> **11 passed**, the same 11 as before the change, with every asserted figure unmoved. A file that had copied the stack would not have noticed.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-drc --test what_the_stack_delivers_against_what_the_net_asked_for` -> **11 passed** before and after. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.

- DONE: **`SignalClass` is gone. Five tables of authoritative-looking numbers that nothing read, and a trait method every rule set had to implement to satisfy them.** 225 lines removed and the workspace builds, tests and gates without a single reference left.
- **Unreachable, and measured before it was touched.** `constraints_for_class` had **no caller anywhere**: every occurrence outside `cypcb-rules` was an *implementation* of the trait method - seven of them, all in test stubs inside `cypcb-autoroute/src`. The language has no way to say a net is high-speed, so nothing could reach it even by hand.
- **What it was carrying: 0.127mm for HighSpeed, 0.2mm clearance, `preferred_layers: vec![0, 2]`, `require_impedance_control: true`.** Numbers with the shape of a standard and no source cited, in a file nothing read. This vector already records the rule for that - a knob that provably does nothing reads like a lever and moves nothing, and the next person spends their fire finding out.
- **Impedance is already stated where a design can state it.** `net CLK [impedance 90ohm]` reaches the model, `ImpedanceRule` measures the stack against it, and `require_impedance_control` was a second way to say the same thing with no way to say it. Deleting it takes nothing away.
- **Two stale NEXT-ACTIONs marked rather than left to be picked up.** V2 still asked for a net-level neck, which shipped in `919b081`; V5 still asked for per-contact clearance reporting, which V1 answered in `ab1e5c9`. Both now carry the commit that closed them.
- **Rule broken, and it cost the run twenty minutes.** A shell loop copied **every** `crates@*.rs` in the scratch directory back into the container - including five files left there by earlier sessions. `registry.rs` and `sync.rs` went back to an older state and the build failed on a field that had been added days later. Recovered with `git checkout --` because the work was committed. **The rule says check the md5 before overwriting the container, and a loop over a glob checks nothing.** Copy named files, one at a time.
- Proof: `grep -rc "SignalClass" crates/ --include=*.rs` -> nothing. `cargo test --workspace --exclude cypcb-desktop` -> clean, including the crate doc example that had to be repaired after the removal cut a line out of the middle of it. `cargo test -p cypcb-autoroute --release --test benchmark_validation -- --ignored` -> 2 passed, ratchets unmoved. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`.
- NEXT-ACTION: **none in this vector again.** What is live across the project: **V7's priority queue** - `core/src/cmp.rs` at 9.45% of the profile, the largest cost left that is not routing arithmetic - and **V1's bigger half**, changing the clearance rule itself to report per contact, which is a re-baseline to time against a publication rather than a heartbeat. Of the two, V7 is the one a single run can finish.

- DONE: **`cypcb export` stopped calling its flag `--preset`, and this vector's list is empty.** One binary spelled two different questions the same way: on `check`, `route` and `score` the flag names a **design-rule table** - what a house can etch - and knows ten fabs; on `export` it named a **file convention** - what a house wants shipped - and knows two. It is `--house` on `export` now.
- **The overlap was the dangerous part and it was already fixed once.** `pcbway` is the one name both lists carry, so exporting with it used to move which rules the board was measured against; `oshpark` is on one list only, so a board written for it could only ever be checked against JLCPCB on the way out. That was corrected earlier by making the pre-export check read the board's own `fab` line. What was left was the name, and a name that answers two questions is the fault `one_word_one_meaning.rs` exists for one level down - `layer top` against `layer Top`.
- **No short form.** `-p` was the short; `-h` is help, so the derived short for `--house` would collide, and `-p` meaning `--preset` on one subcommand and `--house` on another is the confusion the rename removes. The flag is long-form only and the help says why.
- **The refusal message says which of the two lists you are on.** `'oshpark' is not a house this command can cut files for. Two are written down: jlcpcb, pcbway... That is a different list from` `cypcb check --preset`, which knows more names including oshpark. It still fires before the build rather than after the file is read, parsed and imported.
- Proof: `cargo test -p cypcb-cli` -> clean, after six test files and one in-file test moved to the new spelling. The new guard, `one_flag_name_does_not_answer_two_questions`, reads `--help` for four subcommands and checks the **option lines** rather than the prose - `export --help` names the other flag while explaining the difference, which is the point of the prose. Mutation, the flag renamed back to `-p, --preset` -> **2 failed**. `./scripts/quality-gate.sh` -> `=== All stages passed ===`. `README.md` and `docs/SYNTAX.md` updated; `to-kicad --preset` is untouched because there it really is the design-rule table.

- DONE: **the copper pour is computed in one place.** `cypcb_world::copper::fill_zone` is the only code that turns a zone into copper; the Gerber writer and the viewer's snapshot both call it.
